### Shell: in progress
Done: DI composition in the desktop application, `IWindowChrome` with the three
implementations, custom title bar with dragging and buttons, menus projected from the command
registry (native on macOS, in the title bar elsewhere), segmented status bar with ongoing
activity, modal host with backdrop and focus restoration, light/dark/**system themes
as default**, per-module accents, density tokens with compact as default.
**Verified live**: the application starts, the window appears, no errors in the log.

Ribbon done: `RibbonProjection` is **pure logic** next to the registry (testable without
UI), `RibbonView` draws it and knows nothing of registries or contexts. Contextual
tabs are not declared: a tab is contextual when all its commands
require a selection, so the criterion cannot go out of sync.

Command palette and settings done. The **workspace** is done too
(`IDocumentWorkspace`): commands do not create views nor know the window, they ask to
open a document and the shell decides where to put it.

Still missing from the shell: global shortcuts beyond palette and options, tabs for open documents.

### Ledger grid: first version
`GridGeometry` is pure, tested logic: it converts between coordinates and cells and computes what is
visible. With over seventeen billion cells virtualisation is not
an optimisation, it is the only way for the grid to exist. `SheetGridView` draws by hand
instead of using a list control, for the same reason.

Done: headers, selection with a fixed anchor, dragging, keyboard, scrolling,
formula bar that shows the formula and not the result, name box that goes to a
cell, sum/average/count summary in the status bar, sheet tabs.

Missing: in-cell editing (for now it goes through the formula bar), number formats,
draggable widths, frozen panes, copy and paste.

### ODS: first version, verified with the real reference suite
Reading and writing of `.ods`. **Tested both ways with the reference suite installed**: our
files open and formulas compute; files produced by the reference suite are read
with formulas and values.

Two pitfalls of the format, both discovered by actually trying:
- `mimetype` must be the **first** entry of the ZIP and **uncompressed**, otherwise the
  document is not recognisable although it remains a valid ZIP;
- the **OpenFormula** namespace (`xmlns:of`) must be declared: without it, the file opens and the
  values are read, but the reference suite gives `Err:510` on **all** formulas.

ODF formulas do not use our syntax: `of:=SUM([.A1:.A3])` instead of `=SUM(A1:A3)`.
The conversion lives in `OdfFormulaSyntax` and does not touch text inside quotes.

### Formats: ODS and XLSX, verified with the real reference suite
Both read and write, **tested both ways** with the reference suite installed: our
files open and formulas compute, its files are read with formulas and values.

The three formula syntaxes differ and must be converted, otherwise files open
but with all formulas broken:

| | Sheet reference | Argument separator | Prefix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ours | `Dati.B2` | `;` | `=` |
| ODF | `[Dati.B2]` | `;` | `of:=` |
| OOXML | `Dati!B2` | `,` | none |

The conversion never touches text inside quotes: there a comma is user
content, not a separator.

### Cell styles
`CellStyle` is a **value** shared by index: two cells with the same appearance point
to the same style, so a sheet of a hundred thousand identically formatted cells contains one style and
not a hundred thousand. It is also how ODF and OOXML save them, so the model matches the
format instead of having to be translated.

The two formats structure them differently:
- **OOXML** splits the style into four tables — fonts, fills, borders, formats — and
  the cell points to a combination.
- **ODF** declares one style at a time, but distributes the properties over three groups: cell,
  paragraph and text. Horizontal alignment is a **paragraph** property.
- In ODF **naming a font is not enough**: it must be declared in `office:font-face-decls`,
  otherwise the reader silently ignores it. Discovered by testing with the reference suite, which
  discarded Arial without reporting anything.

An empty but formatted cell must not be discarded: the background of a highlighted row is
information, not garbage.

### Formatting commands
Ledger has 27 formatting commands — font, alignment, number formats,
backgrounds and borders — declared like all the others and therefore present in ribbon, menu,
palette and shortcuts without dedicated code.

The link between commands and selection goes through `IActiveSheetContext`: the active view
announces itself, commands ask what to act on. Without that layer every
formatting command would hold a reference to `LedgerView`.

Two rules that look like details but are noticed at once if wrong:
- the style is **derived**, not replaced: bold on an italic cell does not
  turn off italic;
- toggling is decided on the whole selection: if even a single cell is not
  bold, it is turned on for all.

**Startup verification**: checking windows via AppleScript is unreliable.
The application now logs the key moments (`Comandi registrati` (commands registered), `Finestra principale
aperta` (main window opened)) and an exception during composition produces a crash report: without it,
an error would leave the app alive and windowless, without any clue.

### Undo, resizing, frozen panes
`UndoStack` per document — undoing in one sheet does not touch what was done in another.
Transactions group: formatting on three hundred cells is a single undo, and it is undone
**backwards**, which is the only order that truly restores the initial state.
`Push` does not execute the operation: whoever creates it has already modified the document.

Undoing a cell write does not just reapply the content: it goes through the engine, because
a cell's value depends on the others and the calculation must be redone.

Frozen panes: three regions drawn and clipped separately — corner, top
strip, left strip — otherwise scrolling content resurfaces beneath them.
Row and column borders can be grabbed with a tolerance, because hitting a line at one point
with the mouse is impossible.

### Data operations
Copy and paste, find and replace, sorting, filters. They live in
`PulseOffice.Sheets.Engine/Operations` because the hard part is not moving text but
**translating formulas**.

- `FormulaTranslator`: when pasting, relative references shift and those with a dollar
  stay fixed. Outside the sheet they become `#RIF!`. Without this, paste produces
  formulas pointing at the wrong data, which is worse than a visible error.
- Clipboard: internal copy with formulas and styles, plus text on the system clipboard, so one
  can paste outside and from outside. `Incolla solo i valori` (Paste values only) turns formulas into their
  result.
- Search: searching in values and searching in formulas are **two different searches**. A
  cell with `=A1*2` showing 10 is found with A1 only in formulas and with 10 only
  in values.
- Sorting: moves **whole rows**. Sorting a single column would disconnect the data
  from the labels, which is the worst damage a sheet can do silently. Formulas
  that move are shifted, and for equal keys the order is stable.
- Filters: the model computes **which rows do not pass**, the view hides them. The model
  must not know that the concept of a hidden row exists. Hiding preserves the
  original height, otherwise showing again would lose manually set heights.

### Conditional formatting and charts
**Conditional formatting does not modify cells**: it only changes their rendering, and removing
the rule restores the original appearance intact. Rules live in the sheet and apply to a
range; duplicating them on each cell would make them impossible to edit. They are evaluated
by priority, they overlap, and `StopIfTrue` stops the following ones.

Data bars and colour scales are measured on the **rule's range**, not on the single
cell: it is the comparison between values that makes a column of bars readable. The bar leaves
the number readable above it, because replacing it would lose the information.

Charts: the definition says **where** to read from, not what. The chart follows the sheet instead
of photographing it, so changing a number changes the drawing without rebuilding anything. They are
`EmbeddedObject`, so the same chart will live in Folio and in Deck, and the drawing lives in
`ChartRenderer`, separate from the control that hosts it.

Objects on the sheet are anchored to a **cell**, not to a coordinate: inserting a
row moves them along with the data they refer to.

### Persistence of conditional rules and charts (done)
Rules and charts are now saved and read back in **both** formats.

OOXML: `XlsxConditionalMapper` writes `conditionalFormatting` in the sheet and the **differential
formats** (`dxfs`) at the end of the stylesheet — a rule does not impose a complete
appearance, it imposes only what changes. `XlsxChartMapper` writes three aligned pieces: a
`ChartPart` per chart, a `DrawingsPart` with the anchoring to a cell, and the reference from the
sheet. Series carry both the cell references and the cached values: without the former
the chart would be an image, without the latter some readers would show nothing.

ODF: `OdfConditionalMapper` uses the reference suite's extended form
(`calcext:conditional-formats`) and not the specification's style maps, because maps
bind the rule to **one** cell and would multiply automatic styles for each covered
cell. Condition styles are named and end up in `styles.xml`: an automatic
style belongs to the object that uses it and cannot be cited by name. `OdfChartMapper`
writes each chart as a **document of its own** in the package (`Object N/content.xml`), with the
frame anchored inside the cell and the manifest entries.

`OdsWriter` was restructured: content building moved from static methods
to a stateful `ContentBuilder` class, because automatic styles, named styles and
sub-documents now cross different parts of the package. An empty cell hosting a
chart is written anyway: that is where the frame anchors.

**Verified with the real reference suite**, both ways. It found three defects the tests could
not see, because we always only read back what we wrote ourselves:
- The reference suite **encodes style names**: it declares `ConditionalStyle_5f_1` and refers to it
  as `ConditionalStyle_1`. Without decoding, all conditional rule styles
  vanished. Now `OdfStyleMapper` decodes `_XX_` sequences.
- The reference suite **does not declare the overall range** of the chart: it puts addresses
  only on the series. The chart read back pointed to A1. Now their union is computed.
- Bars and columns in ODF are the **same type**: orientation, stacking and percentage
  are style properties of the area, not chart classes. They used to be lost.

Losses declared in `OdsFormat.CheckFidelity`: "stop if true" does not exist in ODF (the
conditions stop at the first true one anyway), and statistical types degrade to columns.

### Geometric shapes: a cross-app object
Shapes are `EmbeddedObject` like charts, so the same shape will live in Folio and in
Deck with no new code. The geometry (`PulseOffice.Drawing/Shapes`) is **normalised 0..1 and
does not depend on Avalonia**: 26 types, each a `ShapeOutline` of figures and segments. Whoever draws
scales it to the size they need — grid, gallery preview, ribbon icon.

**Shape icons are not drawn by hand**: `ShapeIconCatalog` generates them from the same
geometry and exposes them as an `IIconCatalog` added to the hand-written one
(`CompositeIconCatalog`). Adding a shape adds its icon.

`ObjectManipulator` is pure logic: which handle lies under a point (taking
rotation into account), how the box changes when dragging it, at what angle the rotation handle
leads. The grid computes nothing, it draws and asks. Changes go through an event
and are executed by whoever knows how to undo, as for fill.

**ODF: the declared type wins over the path.** Writing `draw:type="round-rectangle"`
the reference suite ignores our `draw:enhanced-path` and redraws the shape with its own formulas
and its own default parameters: the rounded rectangle came out deformed. With a type it
does not know it uses the path, but then converting to XLSX produces `custGeom` and the shape's
type is lost. The way that keeps everything is to declare the **`ooxml-<preset>`** names, which
the reference suite recognises and maps to the OOXML presets: it renders well in ODF and converts to `prstGeom`.
Discovered by actually converting, both ways, and looking at the PDF.

Arcs are flattened into cubics (`ArcFlattener`) because the ODF path has no
equivalent arc command. The tangent angle is derived from the arc's direction and the sign
of the displacements, not from the previous segment: after an `M` there is no previous segment.

A shape with text shrank down to the text: in ODF `draw:auto-grow-height`
is true by default.

**Shell defect found this way**: every `Push` on the undo stack
fired `Changed` on the document, which **reactivated** the document, which **emptied**
the workspace and rebuilt the view. The sheet context detached mid-command —
the just-inserted shape did not appear selected — and with it scrolling,
frozen panes and the edit in progress were lost. Activating a document and updating its facts are now
two distinct events (`ActiveChanged`, `ActiveUpdated`).

### Shape groups and stacking order
A group keeps its children in **relative coordinates** (fractions of its own box), not in
twips: so enlarging the group enlarges the children, and moving it moves them all, without
recomputing anything by hand. `SheetGrouping` converts between the two forms — from the position on the
sheet to fractions and back — and `SheetPlacement` is the piece that measures distances between
cells, because an object is anchored to a cell and not to a point.

The **stacking order** is a datum of the object (`ZOrder`), not the order of the list:
the list changes for a thousand reasons (reading a file, undo, grouping) and tying
the appearance to that order means seeing it change by itself. `ObjectOrdering` is pure logic and
also handles the case that is always got wrong: **several objects brought forward together do not
leapfrog each other**. Drawing and hit-testing use the same order, read once,
otherwise one ends up selecting one object and seeing another react.

Multiple selection is done with **shift and click**; when dragging, resizing and
rotation apply to the primary object, moving to all selected ones.

**Two real defects, found by trying and not by tests:**
- **Objects were drawn in points on a grid measured in pixels.** A 4 cm shape
  occupied three quarters of 4 cm of sheet, and the discomfort was visible only by putting it next
  to the cells. Grouping made it evident, because children ended up shifted
  relative to where they were before. Now `GridGeometry.ToPixels` is used in both directions.
- **Dragging an object up or left, the anchor did not change**: it stayed on the
  starting cell with a **negative** offset, and the part outside the cell vanished
  under the headers. Now moving **re-anchors** the object to the cell containing its
  top-left corner.

Groups and order are saved in both formats: `draw:g` with `draw:z-index` in ODF,
`xdr:grpSp` in OOXML, where the order is the document's order. **Verified with the real
reference suite** both ways: a group written by us, converted by the reference suite and read back, comes back a
group with its two children.

### Context menus have a group title
A separator line says *that* two items belong to different groups, not *which* groups
they are: with twenty items the menu went back to being a list. Now each group carries its own label —
spaced, faint small caps, like the ribbon group labels, because it is the same
role and must read the same way.

The title is not a string written in the menu: it is the **path segment** of the command
(`cell/clipboard` → `context.cell.clipboard`), so it is born already translated into the five languages
and cannot go out of sync with the commands it contains.

Splitting the menu into sensible groups helped more than the graphics: the stacking-order
items were mixed with "edit shape" and "delete object". Now they are
**Object**, **Order** and **Arrange** — three different ideas, three labels.

### Three interface fixes requested by looking at it
**The tab strip did not look like a tab strip.** They were buttons with a
faint pill: they read as text. Now `RibbonTabStrip` draws them — tab with a
rounded top, accent line above the active tab, and the **baseline interrupted
under it**, which is what makes the tab read as attached to the ribbon body. Contextual
tabs are no longer coloured when disabled: they were three green words scattered
among the others, and the colour meant nothing.

**The ribbon no longer collapses the whole group.** Before, when space ran out, a group
vanished behind a button: the most used commands vanished along with the others. Now each group
keeps the first commands visible — those declared first, i.e. the main ones — and sends to the
menu **only those that do not fit**, with the count of how many there are. It collapses entirely
only when not even the minimum fits. Reduction always starts from the group that currently
shows the most commands, so none empties while another stays full.

**The sheet tabs did nothing.** Now they are drawn like the others (tab colour
included) and have the **context menu**, projected from the registry like every other
menu: insert, duplicate, delete, rename, move left and right, tab
colour, protect, hide and show. Double-click renames. Items that make no sense do not
appear: with a single sheet there is no "delete", and "show" appears only if something is
hidden.

A defect of the right kind, found right after: the insert command **created the
sheet twice** — the function describing the change already executed it, and then
`Apply` executed it again. Whoever describes an undoable operation must not touch the document.

### External data: a provider tested against a real database
`QueryRefresher` runs the query and **writes the result into the sheet**: headers,
rows, and cleanup of what the previous run had left further down — without that
cleanup a query that gets shorter leaves old rows indistinguishable from real data. Cell
formatting is preserved: the format was chosen by the user, the content is
brought by the query.

**SQLite was actually tested**, on a file created by the test: types, headers,
written range, shorter second run, unknown connection and broken query. It is the first
of the six providers to be verified against a real database and not against a fake; the
other five require a server and remain untested.

Connections are read from `connections.json` in the configuration folder: the place
where they are written exists, the window to compose them does not — and the refresh command appears
only if the document really has an attached query, because a command that can do
nothing is worse than an absent command.

### Charts: from the six drawn types to the fifty-five of the catalogue
The renderer's `switch` was about to become forty cases: it became a family
of **plotters** (`IChartPlot`), one per group — bars, lines, pie, scatter,
statistical, financial, radar, hierarchies, gauges. The renderer picks the first one that
declares it can draw that type, and whoever adds a family does not touch the others.

**Statistics live in `PulseOffice.Charts`, without Avalonia, and so they are tested**: histogram
bins, five-number summary, outliers beyond one and a half times the
interquartile range, density with a Gaussian kernel and Silverman's rule, cumulative distribution,
theoretical quantiles, running totals. The drawing that follows is then a few lines.

`PlotScale` does one thing only: map a value to a coordinate, and round the extremes
to readable numbers. Axes are no longer drawn by whoever draws the bars: **the plotter
declares its own scale** and the renderer uses it for the grid. Without this, the histogram
showed counts of 2 on an axis going up to 52 — i.e. bars that always touched the
ceiling.

A real defect fixed along the way: selecting **a single column** of numbers the chart
said "no data to plot", because the first column was taken as category and
nothing was left to draw. Now the first column becomes category only if there is more
than one.

### Shapes have the style the formats can describe
There were five options: colour, outline, width, dash, rotation. ODF and OOXML
describe an order of magnitude more, and keeping five meant **losing the rest
on opening someone else's file**. The style is now a tree of records, each with its own
default value:

| Piece | What it carries |
|---|---|
| `ShapeFill` | none, solid, **gradient** (six types, angle, centre, border, stops), **hatch** (single, crossed, triple; angle, distance, background), opacity |
| `ShapeLine` | colour, width, seven dashes, opacity, caps, joins, start and end **arrowheads** |
| `ShapeShadow` | colour, opacity, X and Y offset, **blur** |
| `ShapeGlow` | colour, radius, opacity |
| `ShapeBevel` | five **bevel** profiles and depth |
| `ShapeTextStyle` | font, size, bold, italic, underline, colour, alignment in both directions, wrapping, inner margin, rotation |
| `ShapeStyle.SoftEdge` | soft edges |

**The dialog became four tabs with the live preview beside them**: every change is
seen at once on the shape drawn by the same renderer as the grid, not by an imitation.
The **colour picker** (`ColorPickerView`) has a palette of nine hues by five
intensities plus eight greys, the hex code and the opacity slider.

A defect born from the dialog, and instructive: the colour pickers **turned effects on
by themselves**. The opacity slider notifies its value when the control's template
is applied, i.e. *after* construction, and the handler turned on shadow and glow. Every
shape opened came out with a light-blue halo. Two fixes: the picker announces nothing
before being loaded, and **choosing a colour does not turn the effect on** — that is done by the
checkbox, which is the only thing the user actually pressed.

On screen the shadow **is not drawn with the system effect** but by hand, filling the
same geometry shifted and blurred: `DropShadowEffect` did not appear, and drawing it ourselves also
has the merit of making screen, print and PDF coincide.

**In the PDF a gradient is a real gradient** (`ShadingType` 2 and 3 with an exponential
function), not an average colour, and transparency goes through an `/ExtGState`. Both things
were missing from the PDF because until now no shape knew how to ask for them.

**Verified with the real reference suite, in both formats**: gradient at 45°, crossed hatch,
shape at 50% with its shadow and dash-dot outline open and render as with us.
Losses declared in XLSX: the angle of a **radial** gradient and the angle and distance of the
**hatch** do not exist in OOXML, which has only predefined patterns.

### Connectors and alignment
**A connector has no position of its own**: it derives it from the two objects it joins. The
model keeps the endpoints (`ConnectorEndpoint`: object identifier and side, with
`Automatic` as default) and `SheetConnectors` recomputes the path when something
moves. The automatic side is chosen by comparing the centres: it is the behaviour one
expects without having to declare it.

`ConnectorRouter` is pure logic and knows three forms — straight, elbow, curved. The elbow
between two horizontal sides passes through the middle, between two vertical ones through the middle of the other
direction, and between a horizontal and a vertical it turns **only once**: two bends where one
suffices are noticed immediately.

The computed path is kept **normalised in the connector's box**, so whoever
draws — grid, print, PDF — need know nothing about glue points: it receives an outline as
for every other shape. Arrowheads (`ArrowGeometry`) are built from the direction of the last
segment, not from a stored angle, otherwise rotating the path would make them point elsewhere.

**Alignment and distribution** (`ObjectAlignment`) work on the boxes measured between
cells. Distributing keeps the first and last fixed and equalises the spaces between the edges, not between
the centres: with objects of different widths the eye measures the empty space.

In ODF a connector is `draw:connector` with its endpoints; in OOXML it is `xdr:cxnSp` with the
preset (`straightConnector1`, `bentConnector3`, `curvedConnector3`) and the
`stCxn`/`endCxn` glues, which however name objects by **number**: on reading the
number→name table is rebuilt, because our model binds by name.

### The command palette executed nothing
Pressing Enter the palette closed and **nothing happened**; the same with double-
click. The list row carried a `CommandPresentation` in its `Tag`, while whoever
confirmed looked for a `CommandDefinition`: the comparison never succeeded and the command was
silently lost. `Tag` is `object?`, so the compiler could not notice. Now
the selection is read from a typed list kept next to the rows, and the error is no longer
expressible.

### Vector images: SVG from file
`Inserisci ▸ Immagine SVG…` (Insert ▸ SVG Image…) reads a file, keeps it **in full** in the document and
draws it with the same path as the rest: `SvgPathParser` and `VectorOutlineReader` produce
a `ShapeOutline`, so an icon, a sticker and a shape go through the same renderer
and the same handles. The `viewBox` normalises to 0..1, so scale is a matter for whoever
draws and not for the file.

In ODF the image is a `draw:image` inside a `draw:frame` and the file lives in `Pictures/`, with
its manifest entry. **Recolouring is written into the file**: if it were kept only in the
model, what is seen and what is saved would be two different things, which is the worst
way to lose information.

In XLSX the road of embedded SVG is closed — OOXML demands an SVG **accompanied by
a raster thumbnail**, and we do not have a rasteriser — so the image is saved
as **geometry**: an `xdr:sp` with `a:custGeom` for each path, with its own
fill and outline. One path is one `sp`, because an OOXML shape has a single paint;
the pieces are found again by name (`<id>#<index>`) and become a single object again, with the SVG
rebuilt. The original SVG file is lost, the drawing is kept — which is what is seen.
**Verified with the real reference suite**: the star opens, renders and converts.

### Shapes and images in print and PDF
`IPageCanvas` can now draw a **path** (`DrawPath`), not only rectangles, lines and
text: it is the minimum needed for a shape to exist off screen, and the only way
for preview and PDF to remain the same drawing. The PDF canvas translates the path into
native operators (`m`, `l`, `c`, `h`, `f`/`S`/`B`) inside `q … Q`, with rotation and
mirroring as a `cm` matrix. Arcs are flattened into cubics as for ODF: the
PDF has no arc operator.

**Objects enlarge the printed area.** Before, the area came only from filled cells: a
sheet with a shape and no data printed a blank page, and a shape below the last
written row vanished. `SheetObjectExtent` computes which cells an object covers **from the real
layout**, not from an estimate, and printing merges the two areas.

### Icon and sticker collections
`IAssetLibrary` finally exists as an implementation and not just as an interface, and it is
composed of **sources** (`IAssetSource`) instead of a fixed list:

- `BuiltInAssetSource` exposes as a collection what the application already has — the
  interface icons and the 26 shapes — wrapping the paths in SVG documents. Nothing is downloaded
  and no licence to respect is added;
- `FolderAssetSource` reads the collections **installed by the user**: one folder per
  collection under `raccolte/`, a `pack.json` with name, type and licence, and inside it the
  `.svg` files. A broken or absent manifest does not make the collection vanish: it falls back to the folder
  name. That is how Lucide, Tabler and the others will arrive without the program having
  to contain them.

The licence is shown in the collection picker, because it is a datum of the model and not a
footnote.

**An SVG is not just a path: it is a path with its paint.** The first version
filled everything with the accent, and outline icons — which are `fill="none"` — became
solid blots. Now `VectorDrawing` carries for each path fill, colour and width
of the outline, inherited from ancestors' attributes as SVG prescribes, and the width
is normalised together with the coordinates. Recolouring **does not turn on what was off**:
it replaces the colours present and leaves `none` where it was.

### System menu on macOS: a single instance
`NativeMenu.SetMenu` must be called **only once** per window: Avalonia's native
exporter keeps a reference to the assigned instance and rejects later ones with
`The menu being updated does not match`. Assigning a new one at every context change,
on macOS **opening any document failed** — the most elementary command there
is. Now the menu is created once and its items are replaced
(`CommandSurfaceFactory.FillNativeMenu`).

Found from the log, not from tests: it is a defect that lives only in the native macOS shell and
no UI-less test could see it. Verified by driving the real menu via
AppleScript, checking that the command logs no errors and that the items switch to those
of Ledger.

### Ribbon: three-row layout
A group's commands are laid out in columns of **three rows**, filled by column. With
a single row a group of twenty commands became a strip scrolling horizontally,
with labels cut off above and below: it was not an aesthetic matter, nothing could be found
any more.

The ribbon's height **is not imposed**: the content decides it. It was a constant in the
density tokens, disconnected from the layout, and it took only the two not matching
for the group labels to end up outside. A measure depending on the theme is not
guessed, it is left to be computed.

Clipboard commands removed from the shell: they were placeholders answering "not yet
implemented" and ended up in the same group and on the **same shortcut** as Ledger's real
ones. The clipboard acts on a document's content, so it belongs to the
module, not to the shell.

The icons have arrived: see "Every ribbon command has its icon".

### Multilingual interface: done
The interface speaks the five languages. `PulseOffice.Localization` is a project of its own:
`ITextCatalog` resolves keys into texts, the catalogues are five JSON files **embedded**
in the assembly — a file next to the executable can vanish, and the application would stay mute.

The rule is the same already in force for formulas and format codes: canonical form in one
place only, translation at display time. Applied here it required **removing the
texts from the commands**: a command no longer declares its title, it *names* it, and the
key is **derived from the identifier** (`command.<id>.title`). No key to
invent when a command is added, and no way to let it go out of sync.

Consequence for paths: `MenuPath` and `RibbonPath` were Italian text, now they are **structure
keys** (`home/clipboard`) translated with `menu.*` and `ribbon.*`. The tree is built
by comparing keys and not translated texts, otherwise two different groups that in one
language translate the same would merge.

Fixed along the way a defect the change made evident: the path **contained the
command title**, so every menu item generated a container with a single identical
item inside — "Apri…" (Open…) was a submenu containing "Apri…".

A missing key is shown in angle brackets (`⟦key⟧`) instead of vanishing or
showing as text: that is how the three "Nuovo documento" (New document) commands were discovered, which
built the title from the commercial name. At startup the registry logs the commands
without a translated title, so the next gap is seen before the user does.

Changing language **does not require a restart**: `LanguageCoordinator` binds the setting
to the catalogue, and menus and ribbon are rebuilt, because their titles had been resolved
when they were born. Default: the system language.

The completeness test compares the keys of the five languages: a language that falls
behind breaks nothing and is not seen, it shows English amid Italian until
someone notices. **Verified live** in Italian, German and French,
reading the real system menus and the ribbon.

Still to translate: the texts of specific views (settings, find and replace),
which are a few dozen strings.

### Visual language (first part, done)
Three new pieces, all verified on screen.

**Semantic palette** (`PulseOffice.UI/Theming/Palette.cs`): colours are named by
**role** — surface, raised surface, border, primary text — not by hue. It is
the only way for the dark theme not to become a second application to maintain in
parallel. The dark theme is not the light one inverted: the greys are slightly bluish,
because neutral grey on a dark background tends towards brown, and texts do not reach white,
which dazzles. In the light theme the **sheet is the brightest surface** and the bars are
slightly greyer: the opposite of instinct, but it is the sheet that is looked at for hours.

Views are built in code and not in XAML, so they cannot use
`DynamicResource`: `ThemedElement.Themed(...)` binds a property to a colour and follows its
changes, otherwise every theme change would require rebuilding the views.

**Icons** (`PulseOffice.UI.Icons`, a project of its own because the geometry does not depend on Avalonia):
some seventy paths on a 24×24 grid, drawn here and not taken from an icon
font — for the same reason sticker fonts are converted into paths:
an installed font may be missing, and an interface without icons cannot be used. The keys are the
**command identifiers**: whoever adds a command does not also declare the icon, and a
command without an icon is seen at once because it stays without one. Stroke width is constant and
scales with size.

**Rhythm and scale**: spacing follows a four-point step, text sizes are
derived from `FontSize` instead of being numbers scattered through the views.

Applied to: ribbon (icons, hover and pressed states, separator line),
status bar, formula bar, grid (headers and lines from the palette instead of
transparent greys — it was the only surface not following the theme), start screen.

**Three real defects found while looking at the application, not at the tests:**
- **Modals did not appear.** `DialogHost` built the modal layer and never
  attached it to the visual tree (`_ = window;`, a statement that does nothing). The
  dialogs had never been seen. Now the layer lives in a `FuncControlTemplate`.
- **The order of menus and ribbon was arbitrary**: it came from enumerating a
  `ConcurrentDictionary`. The font group — bold, italic, underline —
  ended up off screen although declared first. The registry now keeps the
  declaration order.
- The three "Nuovo documento" (New document) commands occupied an entire ribbon group while
  working: moved to menu and palette.

The start screen now **works**: the three cards are buttons, not decoration.
The module accent is a line at the top of the card and the icon colour, not a coloured
background: three solid-coloured boxes compete and none of the three can be read.

Not yet verified on screen: the **dark theme**. The palette is complete and tested by the
tests, but seeing it requires changing the Mac's system appearance.

Still missing: document tabs, sheet tabs, command palette and settings and
search views to be polished; collapsing ribbon groups when space is not
enough (today it scrolls horizontally).

### Inert title bar: `VisualRoot` is not the window
The title bar did not drag the window, and neither did minimise, maximise and
close: all went through `VisualRoot as Window`, which **here is null**. The result was a
completely inert bar, with no signal whatsoever — the commands did not fail, simply nothing
happened. It now goes through `TopLevel.GetTopLevel(this) as Window`.

Found by building a tool that synthesises a real drag
(`CGEvent`, some thirty lines of Swift): AppleScript can click but not drag,
and without a real drag there was no way to distinguish "the event does not arrive" from
"the event arrives and does nothing". It was the second case, and the log said so in one line.

The title bar height was also declared in `ExtendClientAreaTitleBarHeightHint` instead of
leaving `-1`: with `-1` macOS kept a strip of about twenty-eight points at the top of the
window, where clicks did not reach our control. Now both zones drag —
the native one of the traffic lights on its own, ours with `BeginMoveDrag`. **Verified**
by measuring the window position before and after.

### Visual identity: the module accent must be used
The first pass was correct but **anonymous**: neutral palette, no colour, three modules
indistinguishable. The accent existed in the model and appeared almost nowhere —
the active ribbon tab was even **blue** while working in Ledger, which is green.

Now the module accent appears where it carries information, not as decoration:
- active ribbon tab, text and line (it was a system resource, the same for all three);
- active sheet tab, as a faint pill;
- **row and column headers touched by the selection**: it is the fastest way to
  know where one is in a large sheet, and before they were indistinguishable from the others;
- pill with dot and module name in the status bar.

The **four-tile logo** that sat in the title bar was removed, and with it the class that
drew it: it said which module one was working in, but that information is already in the window
title, in the accent and in the status bar pill. One more sign at the top of the
window added nothing and took up the most visible place there is.

The palette greys have a hint of blue: perfectly neutral grey on screen
reads as dull, and it is the difference between a sober interface and a dead one.

Group labels are in spaced small caps: a label must read as a
label, not get confused with the command names above it.

Also fixed a key that escaped the conversion: the `Celle` group appeared in the
ribbon as `⟦ribbon.home.Celle⟧` — the marker did its job.

### Ribbon rewritten: real tabs and groups that collapse
The stock `TabControl` was removed: it did not look like a ribbon and did not let us decide
what happens when the groups do not fit. Now the tab strip is built by hand
— tab with a rounded top, module accent on the active tab — and the body is a
panel that **measures the space**.

`RibbonGroupsPanel`: when the groups do not fit, they **collapse** starting from the last
instead of making the bar scroll. A bar scrolling sideways hides commands without
saying they exist: whoever does not know there is more to the right does not look for it. A collapsed group
stays visible, shows icon and name, and reopens in a menu with **the same layout**
it had when open, so one does not have to relearn where a command is. Widening the
window the groups reopen: measurement always restarts from all open.

`RibbonItemFactory` is separate because the same buttons are needed in two places — the open
group and the menu of the collapsed group — and duplicating their construction would mean making them
different sooner or later.

Depth: a barely perceptible gradient on the ribbon background (a uniform plane
reads like paper without thickness), shadow under the bar, faint plate under the main
commands. The sheet tabs are built by hand for the same reason as the others: the
stock theme drew a line that, the tab being as tall as the text, passed
**through** the text.

### Visual direction chosen: crisp in the structure, warm in the moments
Not an average between the two roads — which was what made the interface generic — but a
division with a single rule: **precision is for what works, warmth for what
floats and for what welcomes**. Full table in [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md).

Two radius scales in the tokens, not one: `RadiusTight` for tools (ribbon, grid,
bars) and `RadiusSoft` for floating surfaces (modals, pop-up menus, cards).
Warmth comes from geometry, space and motion, **not from hue**: greys stay
cool, otherwise a technical interface becomes muddy and the accent is no longer noticed.

Done in this pass:
- **Theme of the stock controls** (`PulseTheme.axaml`): fields, lists, checkboxes,
  scroll bars, menus and tooltips. Written in XAML and not in C# because control
  templates in code are unreadable, and that is what XAML exists for. Templates
  are not rewritten: surfaces, radii and states are changed, so as not to inherit the
  maintenance of an entire theme.
- **The module accent reaches the system controls**: `AccentService` also sets
  `SystemAccentColor` and its six variants. Without it, a checkbox in the
  settings stayed **blue** while everything else was green, and the interface revealed itself
  as made of two pieces.
- **Modals had a title and no way to close them**: `options.Title` was not
  drawn anywhere and there was no close button. Now they have
  a header with title and ✕ — verified by clicking it.

### Live tests: the synthetic events trap
**Correction of a wrong conclusion written above earlier.** I had noted
that keyboard events did not reach the application: it is false. They arrive, and so do
clicks. The defect was in the tool, not in the app.

**Before the press a move event must be sent to the target point.** The
native layer resolves the press at the pointer's *current* position, not at the one
declared in the event: without the move the click arrives where the pointer was
before, usually outside the window. The effect is indistinguishable from "synthetic events
do not arrive", and that is the wrong conclusion one reaches.

With the move in front everything works. **Fully verified**: click on a cell
(D6 selected), typing `=2+3` in the formula bar, Enter, and the cell shows
**5** with the cursor moved to D7.

The tools live in [tools/uiprobe](tools/uiprobe) — `click`, `drag`, `keys` — and no
longer in the session folder, which empties between turns. They are needed because UI-less
tests do not see an entire class of defects: in this project they found
the inert title bar, the modals that did not appear and the arbitrary menu order.

### Phase 0 closed
Four things remained, all done and seen on screen.

**Dark theme verified live**, switching it from the interface. It found a defect that
the tests could not see: cell text was **black on a dark background**, unreadable.
The style's default black is not a user choice, it is the absence of a choice, and
taking it literally painted every cell black. Now only a colour actually chosen
prevails over the theme colour.

**Contrast measured, not eyeballed**: a test computes the WCAG ratio between texts and the three
surfaces they sit on, in both themes — 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for
secondary text. It is the only part of the appearance that can be measured.

**Transitions** deliberately short: 120 ms on what is used continuously, 160 ms on what
appears. Longer ones seem elegant the first time and slow the hundredth.

**Settings, search and palette translated.** Settings now follow the same rule
as commands: they no longer declare their texts, they **name** them, and the keys are derived
from the setting's key (`setting.<key>.title`, `.choice.<value>`). Categories
are structure keys (`general/appearance`) translated segment by segment.

Two defects that emerged testing the live language switch:
- an **already open view did not update**: its texts had been resolved when it was
  born. Now `SettingsView` rebuilds itself when the catalogue changes language;
- the **title of a modal** stayed in the previous language, because `DialogOptions` carried
  the already resolved text. Now it carries the **key**, and the header follows.

**Verified live**: changing language from the settings, ribbon, menus, modal
title, labels, descriptions and placeholders all switch instantly — tested in German
and French.

No interface text remains written in the code.

### Phase 1 in progress

**Persistent settings (done).** `JsonSettingsStore` with per-system paths —
Application Support on macOS, `%APPDATA%` on Windows, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` on Linux. **Atomic**
writing (temporary file and replace), because an interruption halfway would leave
the user without preferences *and* with an unreadable file. **Deferred** saving of 600 ms:
dragging a slider must not produce hundreds of writes; on close it writes
immediately, because there is no time to wait there. A corrupted file does not prevent startup.

An instructive defect found by the tests: in `condition ? longValue : doubleValue` the two
branches unify into `double`, so **every saved integer came back as a decimal**. An explicit
cast to `object` is needed.

**Fill by dragging the handle (done).** `SheetFill` is pure calculation on content:
it does not touch the sheet, it says what to write. The rules chosen:
- two or more numbers define a progression, which is extrapolated;
- **a single number repeats**: guessing the step from a single value is almost always
  wrong, and correcting costs more than dragging again;
- an irregular progression (1, 2, 4) is not continued;
- a text ending with a number advances, leading zeros included
  ("Fattura 007" → "Fattura 008");
- formulas are shifted as in paste;
- the rest repeats cyclically.

The grid does not write: it signals `FillRequested` and whoever can undo executes, in **a single
transaction**. The area is shown dashed while dragging, and dragging
diagonally picks the dominant direction, because filling in two directions at once has no
unambiguous meaning.

**Formulas: parentheses only where needed.** `FormulaTranslator` **always** added them: every
copy turned `=A1+B1*2` into `=(A1+(B1*2))`, and after a few fills the formula was
unreadable while remaining correct. Now emission is precedence-aware, mirroring
those of the reader — if they diverged, a rewritten formula would be read back
with another meaning. Two tests encoded the defect and were corrected.

**Verified live**: dark theme set, application closed and reopened, theme still
dark; 1 and 2 written in A1:A2, handle dragged, the column fills 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

**Recent documents (done).** The list lives in its own file and not among the settings:
it changes much more often than a preference, and mixing them would mean rewriting the
settings at every open. Vanished files are not shown — a list of items that do not
open is worse than a short list.

Recents **become commands**, and so appear in menu, palette and search without code
dedicated to each surface: it is the whole reason a command registry exists.
This required two small, justified additions: `CommandRegistry.Unregister`, for
commands that arise from data and change during the session, and `CommandDefinition.TitleOverride`,
**the only exception** to the rule by which a command names its title: a file name
is data, not text to translate.

A defect found by the tests, and important: `RecentDocuments` wrote to the user's **real**
file even during tests, wiping their recent documents. The path is now a
parameter. It was noticed by a test failing for no apparent reason.

### Two new rules, applied to all existing code
**No comments.** Removed from 242 files: 3,235 lines of documentation and 1,581 of comments.
Not with regular expressions — they would have broken strings containing `//` — but with
[tools/strip-comments](tools/strip-comments), which parses C# with Roslyn, removes the comment
*trivia* and reformats the tree. Without the formatter, double indentation remained where the comments
were. Build and 471 tests green after the operation.

**Logs in English.** Twenty-two messages translated, plus the crash report
header. The log is read by developers; the interface stays in the five languages.

### Autosave and recovery (done)
Autosave **does not touch the user's file**: it sets a copy aside in
`ripristino/`, because overwriting without being asked is the fastest way to make them
lose a version. A restored document comes back **modified**, because the file on disk
is still the previous one. The copy is discarded on save, on closing the document and
on clean exit: whatever remains there at startup is, by definition, what a crash
left behind. Closing the window with the ✕ **discards nothing** — it is "I'll decide later",
not "throw away"; only the *Scarta* (Discard) button deletes.

Two real defects, both found by testing live and invisible to the tests:
- **No document ever appeared modified.** `IsModified` was a property nobody
  set: autosave therefore never had anything to save, and the modification
  dot in the title did not appear. Now the state **is derived from the history**:
  `UndoStack.StatePoint` identifies the current state, the document remembers the one at the
  save, and undoing up to that point the document goes back to **unmodified** — which is
  the right behaviour and one a boolean flag cannot give.
- **`OdsSpreadsheetReader.CanRead` did not recognise a single ODS file**, not even ours:
  it read 38 bytes and looked for `opendocument` in them, which in the package is found around the
  sixtieth. Nobody had noticed because opening from file falls on
  `ReaderFor(path)`, which looks at the extension; content-based recognition only serves
  whoever has no extension — that is, precisely recovery.

**Fully verified live**: value written, wait for autosave,
`kill -9`, restart, recovery dialog, *Ripristina* (Restore), and the cell comes back with its
content, the document marked as modified and "Documenti ripristinati: 1" (Documents restored: 1) in the status
bar.

### The modal veil: alpha written backwards
Modals **already had** a veil, and it was never seen. Colours with transparency were
written in CSS order (`#RRGGBBAA`), while Avalonia reads `#AARRGGBB`: the light veil
`#0F172459` became a blue at **6% opacity**, and the dark one `#00000099` was
**completely transparent**. The same error was in `Hover` and `Pressed`, so the hover
and pressed states were almost invisible too — the interface seemed not to react.

Six colours corrected, and two tests that now **measure the alpha channel** instead of trusting the
string: the veil between 0x80 and 0xE0, hover barely perceptible, pressed
necessarily stronger than hover. A colour written backwards can no longer
go unnoticed. The veil appears in 160 ms instead of abruptly.

**Verified on screen in both themes**, opening the settings: the window behind really
darkens.

### Numeric settings: reading by value, not by type
`Get<long>` on a setting whose factory value is an `int` **crashed the
application at startup**: the fallback was a direct cast to the requested type. A number read
from JSON may arrive as `int`, `long` or `double` depending on how it was written, so
the exact type is not information to rely on. Now numeric types are **converted**
between each other, while a text never becomes a number: that remains a value of the wrong type, and
falls back to the factory value as before.

### Printing and PDF export (done)
Four new pieces, each with a single responsibility.

**`PulseOffice.Printing`** — pure pagination, without Avalonia and without knowing what a
spreadsheet is: paper sizes, orientation, margins, headers and footers with fields (`&P`, `&N`,
`&D`, `&F`, `&A`), and `BandPaginator`, which breaks a band of items of differing size into
pages. Rows and columns use **the same paginator**: they are the same problem in two
directions, and writing it twice would mean fixing it only once. An item larger
than the page takes a page of its own instead of vanishing, and rows to repeat
take space from **every** page, not only the first.

**`IPageCanvas`** is the boundary between "what to draw" and "where": the printable document paints
on an abstract surface, and whoever provides it decides whether it becomes a PDF or an on-screen
preview. Without this boundary the preview would be a second implementation of the drawing,
i.e. a second set of defects.

**`PulseOffice.Formats.Pdf`** — we write the PDF ourselves, like ODF, and for the same reason:
objects, cross-reference table, streams compressed with `FlateDecode`, the fourteen standard
fonts with WinAnsi encoding. The **glyph widths** are really needed: without them one cannot
right-align nor cut a text that is too long. Accented letters are measured like
their bases — in Helvetica `é` is as wide as `e` — so a table for every
language is not needed.

**`PulseOffice.Sheets.Printing`** joins the two: sheet pagination, row and column
headers, grid, borders, backgrounds, alignment and colours of number formats.

**Column widths moved into the model.** They lived only in the grid, in pixels:
printing could not see them and no format could save them. Now `Worksheet.Layout` keeps
them in twips and `GridGeometry` converts. Intended consequence: **each sheet has its own**,
while before a single grid served all the sheets of the document.

**Real printing**: `IPrintService` in `PulseOffice.Platform`. The document becomes a temporary
PDF and then goes to the system — CUPS (`lp`) on macOS and Linux, the shell print verb on
Windows. Printer discovery **cannot read `lpstat -p`**: that text is translated
("la stampante X è in attesa" (printer X is idle)), and `LC_ALL=C` is not enough because on macOS CUPS translates
itself. `lpstat -e` is used, which prints only the names.

**Verified live in three ways**: reading our PDFs back with **PDFKit**
([tools/pdfprobe](tools/pdfprobe)) instead of our own code; looking at the rendered
page; and using the application — new sheet, *Esporta in PDF…* (Export to PDF…), save, and the
file read back shows header, content and "1 / 1" in the footer. The printer list
in the print dialog is this machine's real one.

Declared limits: only the standard fonts, so texts outside Latin-1 (Greek,
Cyrillic, CJK) become `?` until a subset TrueType is embedded; text that
does not fit in a cell is **clipped** instead of overflowing onto the empty cells beside it,
as spreadsheets do.

### The ribbon emptied when writing in a cell
*File* and *Annulla* (Undo) remained. The command context has two sources — the facts of the
**document** (open, modified, can undo) and the facts of the **view** (what is
selected) — and `Activate` **rebuilt it from scratch** at every change, wiping
`HasSelection` along with the selection. All the commands acting on a selection
vanished, i.e. almost all. Now `Activate` replaces only the document's facts and leaves
the others intact.

### Global shortcuts and zoom (done)
**A shortcut is no longer an `if` in the window.** Before there was a single hand-written
case (the palette with ⇧⌘P) and the shortcuts declared by commands reached nowhere.
Now `ShortcutDispatcher` asks the registry which gestures are active *in this
context* and resolves the pressed key: whoever adds a command with `DefaultGesture` gets the
shortcut, the menu item with its symbol and the row in the shortcuts window,
without touching anything else.

Three decisions noticed only if wrong:
- **`Ctrl` in the declaration means "the primary modifier"**: ⌘ on macOS, Ctrl
  elsewhere. Declaring the same command twice for two systems is the sure way to make them
  diverge.
- Listening is in **tunnel**, not bubble: otherwise the grid, which has focus, consumes
  the key before the shell sees it. So as not to steal typing, a key **without
  modifiers** is never a shortcut — except function keys.
- The **same** parsing serves menus, palette and shortcuts window. Before, the
  menus used Avalonia's `KeyGesture.Parse` and the palette showed the raw string: three
  surfaces, three different answers for the same command.

**Sheet zoom** (25%–400%): scale transform on the drawing, with pointer
coordinates divided by the zoom. The model's measures are not touched, so zoom cannot
dirty the column widths — which are now document data. ⌘+, ⌘−, ⌘0 and
⌘wheel; the indicator is in the status bar.

**The status bar did not follow its own model.** Segments notify changes
(`INotifyPropertyChanged`), but the view redrew only when someone else called
`Refresh`: messages appeared late or never. Now the service announces changes and
the view updates itself, on the UI thread — the timed message expires on a
timer, i.e. off that thread.

**Verified live**: ⌘+ twice goes to 120% and the grid really grows, ⌘− twice
to 80%, F1 opens the shortcut list with the ⌘ ⇧ symbols, the search "zoom" leaves three
rows, ⇧⌘P opens the palette.

A trap of the tools, not of the app: `uiprobe` key codes are **physical
positions**. With an Italian layout code 27 (`-` on an American keyboard) arrives as
`'`, and `-` is at 44. It seemed ⌘− did not work; it was the keyboard. Noted in
[tools/uiprobe](tools/uiprobe).

### Phase 2: pivot tables (done)
The model was there, the engine was not. Now everything is there: `PivotEngine` crosses rows and columns,
`PivotAggregator` does the fifteen aggregations, `PivotGrouping` groups dates and numeric
ranges, `PivotRenderer` writes the table into the sheet and `PivotCoordinator` keeps it
aligned with the data.

Three choices that decide whether the numbers are right:
- **Subtotals are computed from the data, not by summing the underlying totals.** With sum
  the difference is not seen; with average, median or distinct count the result
  would simply be wrong.
- Percentages and running totals are measured **on the items**, excluding subtotals and
  grand total: otherwise every percentage would be worth half of what it should.
- Recalculating **first clears the written area**: a table that shrinks would
  otherwise leave the old rows beneath it, indistinguishable from real data.

Definitions live in the **document** (`Workbook.Pivots`), like conditional rules and
charts, so they can be saved in the formats; the calculation lives in `PulseOffice.Sheets.Pivot`,
which does not know the interface. A destination inside the source data is rejected: it would be
a table eating its own numbers.

**Verified live**: data entered in the app, *Dati → Tabella pivot* (Data → Pivot table), fields assigned to
row/column/value, and on the new sheet appear Nord 130, Sud 90, Dado 100, Vite 120,
total 220, with totals in bold.

Two defects found while testing:
- **Sheet tabs did not follow the document**: a sheet added by code (like
  the pivot's) did not appear until the document was reopened.
- **Global shortcuts stole keys from text fields.** With tunnel listening,
  ⌘A inside the cell editor executed the sheet's "select all" instead of selecting the
  text. Now, when focus is in a text field, the field sees the key first and the
  shell intervenes only if it stays unhandled.

### Phase 2: analysis and sheet structure (done)
**Goal seek** (`GoalSeek`): secant method on the value of the formula
cell, with the variable cell **put back as it was** at the end — the search tries dozens of
values, and leaving a random one would be worse than not having it.

**Multiple operations** (what-if tables): a column of inputs, a row, or both
crossed. Input cells are restored as in goal seek.

**Scenarios**: a named snapshot of a group of cells. Applying one returns the previous
values, so the operation is undoable without remembering anything elsewhere.

**Solver**: Nelder–Mead with penalties on constraints (≤, =, ≥, integer, binary) and variables
non-negative by default. No external library: it is a direct
optimiser, suited to small problems like those written in a sheet. Tested on a
parabola, on a maximum constraint, on x·y with x+y=10 (gives 5 and 5), on a cube root and on an
integer constraint.

**Rows and columns are inserted and deleted** — it was missing entirely, and it is an
elementary operation. The hard part is not moving cells but **rewriting formulas**:
- insertion also moves **absolute** references: `$A$5` becomes `$A$7` if
  two rows are inserted above, because the dollar locks copying, not structure;
- a range that *contains* the insertion point **widens**, instead of shifting;
- deleting makes `#REF!` only references to the vanished cells, while ranges
  shrink;
- formulas on **other sheets** are touched only if they name the modified sheet.

To do it a hierarchy was extracted: `FormulaRewriter` walks the tree and renders the text,
`OffsetRewriter` is the paste shift, `StructureRewriter` is the structural rule.
Before, the rewriting logic lived inside the paste translator, and a second rule
would have meant a second copy of the renderer.

Heights, widths, anchored objects and conditional rules also move; an object or a
rule lying entirely in the deleted rows vanishes with them.

Undo goes through `SheetSnapshot`: a structural change touches cells, others'
formulas, measures, objects and rules, and the point inverse does not exist — a formula that became
`#REF!` does not remember what it pointed to.

**Verified live**: 10, 20 and `=A1+A2` in a column, insertion of a row above the
second, the formula becomes `=A1+A3` and still gives 30; ⌘Z puts everything back as it was.

### Phase 2: data tools and validation (done)
**Remove duplicates**, **text to columns**, **subtotals** and **consolidation** are
pure calculation: they return a *plan* (which rows to remove, which values to write, which
formulas to insert) and do not touch the sheet. Whoever uses them decides when to apply it and knows how to
undo it — the same separation as filters, where the model says which rows do not pass and
the view hides them.

Details that matter:
- text to columns respects **quotes**: `"Rossi; Ada";Torino` makes two fields, not three,
  and `""` inside quotes is a single quote;
- subtotals produce `SUBTOTAL` formulas, not values: they stay live if the data changes, and that is
  the reason SUBTOTAL ignores other subtotals;
- consolidation **by label** aligns items that in the source sheets are in different
  order, which is the whole point compared to consolidation by position.

**Data validation**: integer, decimal, list (also from a range), date, time, text
length and custom formula, with the three alert levels. Only *Stop* actually prevents
writing: the other two warn and let the user decide, and it is a difference to be respected
or validation becomes a cage.

For the custom formula the engine now has `EvaluateExpression`, which evaluates an expression
on the fly in the context of a cell without writing it anywhere.

Also added to the model: `SheetProtection` and per-sheet validation lists.

### Phase 2: sheet structure and statistics (done)
**Print areas, rows to repeat and groupings** are now sheet data, and follow
insertion and deletion of rows and columns along with comments, objects and rules. Printing
of several areas goes through `CompositePrintDocument`, which chains printable documents: it is needed
already now for multiple areas and will be needed to print several sheets together.

Collapsing a group **remembers the measures** of the rows it hides: without that, reopening it
would give back rows all the same and the work of whoever had sized them would be lost.

**Protection and validation act on writing**: a locked cell on a protected sheet
rejects the edit, and a value outside the rules is stopped only if the alert is of type
*Stop* — the other two warn and let writing happen, as the format prescribes.

**The thirteen statistical procedures** of the reference suite: descriptive, correlation, covariance, one-factor
ANOVA, t-test (paired and two-sample, with and without equal variances), F-test, z-test,
chi-square, moving average, exponential smoothing, regression, Fourier analysis and
sampling. Probability values reuse the numeric functions already written for the
sheet functions — regularised incomplete beta and gamma — instead of a second
implementation that sooner or later would give different numbers from the same formulas.

The procedures **translate nothing**: they return rows with a label *key*
(`statistics.mean`), and whoever shows them translates. It is the same rule as commands and pivots.

Two details the tests clarified: a paired difference **without variance** has no
t value (Excel gives `#DIV/0!`, we give `NaN`), and an F equal to zero has probability 1, not undefined.

### Phase 2: advanced filters, sort lists, comments (done)
**Advanced filter** with a criteria range, as in the reference suite: criteria on the **same row**
apply together, different rows apply as alternatives. A criteria column that does not
match any header of the data is ignored instead of hiding everything.
Extraction of unique values only was added too.

**Custom sort lists**: jan, feb, mar are not in alphabetical order, and without
lists a sheet of months sorts senselessly. What is not in the list ends up at the
bottom, not at the top. `ISortLists.ContainingAll` recognises the right list from the selected
values, which is how the reference suite proposes it by itself.

Sorting and filtering were **static** classes from before the dependency
injection rule: they became `ISheetSort`/`SheetSorter` and `ISheetFilter`/`SheetFilterService`,
injected like everything else.

**Cell comments**: red corner in the cell, pop-up text when hovering over it, dialog
to write them, undo. They move with rows and columns like the other anchored objects.

**Verified live**: comment written on A1, red corner appeared, and hovering with the
pointer one reads "user: Da confermare con l'ufficio" (To be confirmed with the office). To test it we needed to
add to `uiprobe` a move **without click**: a click closes the pop-up
tooltip, so with a click alone it would never have been seen.

### Phase 2: the analysis dialogs (done)
Goal seek, solver and scenarios now have their dialog.
`FormPromptView` builds a form from a list of fields (text, number, choice, checkbox):
five almost identical hand-written dialogs would have become five maintenance burdens, and
none would have stayed the same as the others.

Solver constraints are written **one per line** (`B1<=10`); a reference alone
means "integer". It is the most direct form to type, and can be replaced with a table
when needed.

**Verified live**: `A1=2`, `A2==A1*7`, goal seek for 91 → A1 becomes **13** and A2
shows 91.

Two defects found and fixed:
- `MinHeight = double.NaN` **crashes Avalonia** (unlike `Width` and `Height`, which
  accept it as "not set"). The dialog did not open at all.
- the key `menu.data.analysis` was missing: the menu showed `⟦menu.data.analysis⟧`, which is
  exactly the marker's job.

And one in the test tool, not in the app: the **first typed character was always
lost**, both when opening a cell and when entering a freshly focused field. Now `keys` first sends
a shift press, which writes nothing and wakes up the event queue.

### Phase 2: the new stuff really gets saved (in progress)
Comments, validations and print areas now **survive saving**, in ODS and XLSX, and
the round trip was tested with the **real reference suite** in both formats.

A trap found only by trying: in ODF the argument separator in validation
conditions is the **comma** inside `cell-content-is-between(1,10)`, but the **semicolon**
inside `cell-content-is-in-list("Nord";"Sud")`. With the semicolon in both, the reference suite
**silently discarded** the numeric validation and made the cells point to the remaining one: a
document that opens, looks right and has lost a rule. Discovered by writing three variants
of the same condition and asking the reference suite which survived.

In OOXML the pitfall was different: the SDK's enumerated values (`DataValidationValues.Whole`) do not
compare as strings — `ToString()` gives `Whole`, not `whole` — and validation came
back as "any value". Now the comparison is on values, not on text.

Difference between the two formats, declared: **XLSX keeps the validation range**
(`A2:A10` stays so), **ODF rebuilds it from the marked cells**, so after a round trip through
the reference suite it shrinks to the non-empty cells. It is the format, not a defect of ours.

**Measures and groupings are saved** in both formats: column widths, row
heights, hidden rows and columns, outline groups with their open state.

A defect was lurking here: in ODF the rows of a group live **inside**
`<table:table-row-group>`, and the reader walked only the table's direct children. A file
with grouped rows would have lost the data of those rows — not the appearance, the **data**. Now
reading traverses groups recursively.

In OOXML groups do not exist as elements: there is an `outlineLevel` on each row and column, and the
group is **rebuilt** from runs of adjacent rows with the same level. A group is
considered collapsed when all its rows are hidden, which is exactly what Excel
writes.

**Verified with the real reference suite**: width 4 cm, height 1 cm, group on rows 3-5 and
all six cells come back intact.

**Pivot tables are saved in ODF** as `table:data-pilot-tables`, and the reference suite really
recognises them: reopening the file it rewrites them adding its own attributes
(`table:buttons`, the field levels), a sign that it interpreted them and did not just copy them.

**Scenarios** stay in memory for a declared reason: in ODF a scenario is not a
set of values with a name, it is a **hidden sheet** duplicating another one. Translating our
model into that form is a real conversion, not a mapping, and writing it halfway
would give files the reference suite opens and mangles.

### External data: the providers tested, passwords out of the document (done)
The six providers now exist **and work**: five were tested against real servers
in Docker on this machine (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle). The tests are
in `PulseOffice.Data.Tests` and **skip themselves** when the port does not answer: a test
that requires a server must not break the build of whoever does not have that server.
They test connection, wrong credentials, table list, column types,
parameters (with a value containing `'; DROP TABLE`) and truncation at the row limit.

Oracle listed **2,044 tables**: `all_objects` contains the data dictionary. Now
system schemas are excluded and the user's two remain. No test saw it because
no test had ever talked to a real Oracle.

**Passwords live in the operating system keychain**, never in the document and never in the
connections file. `ISecretVault` in `PulseOffice.Platform` with three implementations —
`security` on macOS, `secret-tool` on Linux, Credential Manager via `advapi32` on Windows —
and a session fallback when none is available, which keeps the secret in memory and
forgets it on exit: better to ask for it every time than to write it in clear text. **Verified
live**: written, read back and removed from this Mac's real keychain, and `connections.json`
contains only the credential name.

**The clear-text password is a choice, not a default.** A checkbox in the
connections dialog writes it into `connections.json`, and ticking it shows a
red warning saying who will be able to read it: without that line the checkbox would be a trap,
because the risk is not seen until it is too late. The secret lives **in one place only** —
choosing the file, the keychain entry is removed; removing the choice, the password
goes back to the keychain and vanishes from the file. Saving again without retyping the password
keeps it as it was, in both cases.

Connections are now **written**, not only read: `FileConnectionDirectory` saves
atomically and `IConnectionDirectory` moved up into `PulseOffice.Data`, because a connection
is not spreadsheet stuff — Folio and Deck will want it too.

**The data table is a cross-app object.** `DataTableObject` is an `EmbeddedObject` like
charts and shapes: it carries the query definition **and** the last result, so a
document opens and reads even without network. `DataTableLoader` (in `PulseOffice.Document.Data`)
turns a query into a snapshot, `DataTableRenderer` draws it, and neither knows
what a sheet is: when Folio and Deck arrive the table will already be there.

`PulseOffice.Data.UI` is the project the three applications will share: the connections
dialog (create, edit, test, delete) and the import dialog (connection → table
or SQL → preview → insertion). The connection editor is **inside** the dialog, not in
a second modal: modals do not nest. *Prova* (Test) saves before testing, because the
password being typed lives in the keychain and not in the form.

In Ledger import creates a `QueryBinding` at the selection anchor, refreshes it and
registers it: the link stays live and *Aggiorna i dati esterni* (Refresh external data) reads it again.

**Imported dates carry their format.** Before, a `timestamp` column arrived as a
serial number — `44616,44625` instead of a date — because the value was converted and the
style was not. Now writing derives the cell format from the value's type (14 for dates,
22 for date and time).

**Real defect found live: undo did not redraw.** The model really went back,
but the grid kept showing the previous data — i.e. the screen lied. Point
edits were noticed because they went through `RequestRefresh`; a restore from a
snapshot did not. Now it is **the view that follows the history** (`UndoStack.Changed`), which is the
right place: it holds for every command, including those to come.

**Fully verified live**: PostgreSQL connection created from the interface, *Prova* (Test)
answers «Connessione riuscita» (Connection successful), the list shows the real tables of the `shop` schema,
the preview shows the rows, *Inserisci* (Insert) brings them into the sheet with headers and formatted
dates, ⌘Z empties the sheet and ⇧⌘Z fills it again. The clear-text password choice was also tested
live, both ways: ticked, the password appears in the file and vanishes from the
keychain, and *Prova* answers «Connessione riuscita» reading it from there; unticked, it goes back to the
keychain and the file stays clean.

### Ribbon buttons have no background of their own
Every button showed a greyish rectangle even at rest: in the ribbon it was the "faint plate"
declared under the main commands, in the pop-up menu it was the default background of the stock
theme. A permanent background under every command breaks the strip into many boxes and strips
meaning from the pointer hover, which is the only moment a background should appear.

The background was declared **twice and in two places**: styles built in code inside
`RibbonView` and nothing elsewhere. Those styles however live in the ribbon's visual tree, and a
pop-up menu lives in a popup, i.e. **outside**: its buttons fell back on the stock theme.
Now the rule lives once only in the theme (`Button.ribbon` in `PulseTheme.axaml`) and applies wherever the
button appears; `RibbonItemFactory` just declares the class.

### The context menu floats too, so it has its shadow
The submenu does not go through the `ContextMenu` template: it is a popup declared inside the
`MenuItem` template, so the surface must be dressed there. Two things discovered by trying, because neither of the
two can be guessed:
- **the child of a `Popup` cannot be reached with the child combinator** (`Popup > Border`):
  that border lives in the `PopupRoot`, not under the `Popup`. It is reached by exclusion —
  `MenuItem /template/ Border:not(#PART_LayoutRoot)` — because in the template there are two borders and
  the other has a name;
- **there are two painting surfaces**, and the inner one is on top: dressing only ours
  left the grey rectangle of the stock theme. Turning the inner one off, however, makes everything depend on a
  selector that, as seen, may not match — and then the menu becomes **transparent**.
  The inner one therefore receives the palette colours (`Palette.Apply` binds `MenuFlyoutPresenter*` to
  `SurfaceOverlay` and `Border`, and sets `OverlayCornerRadius`): if the selector misses, the surface
  is the right one anyway, and the shadow is the only thing lost.

The margin making room for the shadow is **only on the right and bottom**: uniform, it shifted the menu from the
point where one presses and the submenu from the item opening it. The shadow falls there, because light comes
from above.

Same rule as the ribbon pop-up menu, and same trap: the popup clips its own
content, so a shadow declared on the outer border is not seen. The `ContextMenu` template
is now a surface with its own margin — the space in which the shadow exists — inside a
transparent `ContextMenu`. The margin shifts the menu a few points relative to the pointer: it is the
price of the shadow, and it is smaller than the damage of a menu that looks glued to the sheet.

### Coverage of the reference suite's spreadsheet: 373 of 373 (100%)
The last six: signing an existing PDF and the five commands that were stuck halfway.

**Signing a PDF is not signing a file**: the signed document must remain **the same
document**, so it is not rewritten — an incremental update is **appended** with
the signature object, the form field and an updated catalogue, plus a cross-reference
table pointing to the previous one with `/Prev`. The signature is a detached PKCS#7
(`SignedCms`) on the file content **excluding the space of the signature itself**: that is what
`/ByteRange` declares, and the hole in the middle is the only way a signature can sit inside what it signs.

**A real, instructive defect, found only with a real reader.** Our tests passed and
PDFKit **rejected the file**: rewriting the catalogue I was **inventing its content**
(`/Pages 2 0 R` fixed) instead of preserving it, so the signed document pointed to a page
tree that did not exist in that file. Now the original catalogue is read, `/AcroForm` is added to it
and the rest stays intact — and a test watches over it. It is the same lesson as
[tools/pdfprobe](tools/pdfprobe): reading back only what we write is not enough.

**The five partial ones**: the **series** dialog (arithmetic, geometric, dates with
weekdays and months, stop value) on top of a new, tested engine; **move or copy sheet** with
real duplication; the three-condition **standard filter**, which finally applies the filter engine
written long ago; document **structure protection**, with the password
kept as a hash and never in clear text; and **macro organisation** (rename, duplicate,
delete) on top of the document library.

### The scattered items: ninety commands in one go (done)
Coverage from 277 to **367 of 373 (98.4%)**. `SignPDF` and five partial items remain.

The bulk are short commands on engines already written, but some required a new model:
**random numbers** with five distributions and shuffling, **label ranges**, **sheet
events** hooked to macros, **right-to-left direction**, **set of selected sheets**.

**We write the QR code ourselves** (`QrEncoder`): version 4 with M correction, byte encoding,
Reed–Solomon over GF(256), mask and format. One more library for a square of thirty-three
cells is not justified, and the result is an SVG that goes through the same renderer as everything
else.

**Font effects**: double underline, overline, superscript, subscript, shadowed,
outlined. Drawing in the grid uses text decorations where they exist and draws them by
hand where they do not (double underline is two lines, shadow is the repeated text).

**Defect found only by the real startup**, for the third time: `IPrintService` is not registered in the
container — it goes through `IPrintServiceProvider` — and the application did not start. Tests do not
compose the container; only startup composes it.

### OOXML aligned with ODF (done)
The gap was there, and it was worse than "not yet": XLSX's `CheckFidelity` declared **a single**
loss, so the format lost things **silently** — which is the defect this project
considers the worst.

Brought into XLSX: **font effects** (double underline, shadow, outline, superscript and subscript),
