**scenarios** (`<scenarios>` with `<inputCells>`), **sparklines** (extension `x14:sparklineGroups`),
**sheet direction**, **free paths** (as `custGeom`, the same road as SVGs) and
**form controls** (`ControlPropertiesPart` with `x14:FormControlProperties`).

Declared what OOXML cannot describe, instead of losing it covertly: non-VBA macros, macro
signature, cell language, overline, editable path nodes, signature lines,
sheet and control events, label ranges. These are nine new losses in
`CheckFidelity`, each with its own code.

**Verified with the real reference suite**: an XLSX written by us with superscript, double underline,
shadow, a scenario and a sparkline, converted by the reference suite and read back, comes back with everything in its
place. Form controls survive **our** files but not the round trip through the reference suite, which
rewrites controls its own way: it is declared as a loss.

### Digital signature (done, except PDF)
Coverage from 274 to **277 commands of 373 (74.3%)**. Signing and verification of the ODF document, macro
signing, signature line. **Not done: signing an existing PDF** — it is a subsystem of its own
(incremental update of the file with `/ByteRange` and PKCS#7), and promising it halfway on a signature
would be worse than declaring it absent.

**We write the signature ourselves**, like ODF and PDF, because the delicate part is not the algorithm but
*what* is signed. `System.Security.Cryptography.Xml` is used only for canonicalisation, which is
the piece where our own implementation would surely go wrong; the rest — which package
entries go into the signature, the digests, the value — is ours and tested.
Provisioning note: version 10.0.0 of the package is flagged with known vulnerabilities, so the
pinned version is **10.0.12**.

**The content is signed, not the container.** All package entries go into the signature
except `mimetype` and `META-INF/`: the first cannot change (it is the format recognition) and the
second contains the signature itself. Verification does not just recheck the declared
digests: **it also checks that no new entries have appeared**, otherwise one could
add a sheet to a signed document and the signature would remain valid.

The **signing time** is signed too: the date lives in a `SignatureProperty` which is itself
a signed entry. Without it, the date would be a label anyone could modify.

**Macros are signed separately**, on the digest of their content, sorted by name because
the order of a dictionary is not a fact of the document. It serves the rule already written in the permissions
model: a macro signed by someone known can have more freedom than an anonymous one.

The status distinguishes four cases, and the difference matters: **valid**, **the document changed after
signing**, **untrusted certificate** (a self-signed one, which is still a real signature),
**expired certificate**. Confusing them would mean saying "invalid" to a good signature made with a
certificate nobody has counter-signed.

Certificates come from the **system keychain** (22 personal ones on this machine) or from a
`.pfx` file with its password, which is not kept anywhere.

**Verified**: an `.ods` written and signed by us reopens with the signature recognised, and
**the reference suite opens and converts it without complaints**; tampering with the content, adding a
part or changing the declared date, verification says *broken*. The signature line on the sheet was
verified on screen. Not verified: that the reference suite's signatures panel shows ours —
it requires signing with the reference suite for comparison, which cannot be done without a UI.

### Spelling, thesaurus, hyphenation and autocorrect (done)
Coverage from 268 to **274 commands of 373 (73.5%)**. Spell checking with real dictionaries,
wavy underline while typing, thesaurus, hyphenation, language per cell and
per document, autocorrect.

**The engine is `WeCantSpell.Hunspell`**, a pure C# port: no native binary, so the
multiplatform constraint holds without `#if` and without a package per architecture. Verified by
reflection before adopting it — it references only the base library — as was done for the
scripting engines.

**We do not ship the dictionaries.** They are `.aff`/`.dic` files the user already has: the locator
looks for them in its own configuration folder and then in the system locations of the three operating
systems, those of other office suites included. On this machine it finds **thirty** without the user installing
anything. Shipping them would have meant choosing which languages deserve to be in the program and weighing
tens of megabytes for the others.

**The split between the two projects is that of scripting**: `PulseOffice.Text.Spelling` holds the
abstractions and pure logic — tokenizer, autocorrect, hyphenation according to Liang,
reading of the MyThes format — and depends on nothing; `PulseOffice.Text.Spelling.Hunspell` is
the adapter touching files and the package. So the part that decides *what an error is* is
tested without dictionaries and without UI.

**The tokenizer decides what is worth checking**, and it is the part noticed if
wrong: the apostrophe and hyphen keep the word together (`dell'anno`, `socio-economico`),
numbers and alphanumeric codes are skipped, and **e-mail addresses and links are skipped
entirely** — otherwise `mario@example.org` would become three errors.

**Language is a property of the cell** (`CellStyle.Language`), with a document default
value and fallback to the system language. In ODF it travels as `fo:language` and `fo:country`
in the style's text properties, which is where the formats really put it.

**The red waves are drawn the same way as the text**: the prefix up to the start
and end of the misspelt word is measured with the same `FormattedText` that draws the cell, so the
underline sits under the right word even with a different font or a right-aligned cell.
Formulas and numbers are not checked: an error on `=SOMMA(A1:A3)` would be noise.

**Autocorrect acts on cell confirmation**, not while typing: correcting
under the fingers while writing in a grid is intrusive, and at confirmation the text is complete.
The rules are the usual ones — known replacements, sentence capital, two initial capitals,
typographic quotes, dash — and each can be turned off.

**Verified live**: «Questo e un testoo sbagliaato» shows red waves under the two invented
words and not under the others; *Sinonimi…* (Synonyms…) on «casa» proposes «abitazione (s.f.)» from the real
Italian dictionary. Also verified outside the application: the thirty dictionaries, hyphenation
(`meraviglioso` → `me-ra-vi-glio-so`) and the English synonyms.

### Interactive drawing (done)
Coverage from 259 to **268 commands of 373 (71.8%)**. Polygon, 45° polygon, curve and freehand
line — each empty or filled — plus point editing and guide lines.

**The path is made of nodes, not segments.** A `FreeformPath` keeps nodes with their two
handles and a type (corner, smooth, symmetric), and the `ShapeOutline` to draw is **derived**: if
we kept both, the point editor and the renderer would go out of sync at the first
move. The model lives in `PulseOffice.Drawing/Freeform`, does not know Avalonia, and construction,
editing and normalisation are tested without UI.

**The freehand line is simplified** (Ramer–Douglas–Peucker) before becoming a curve: a
drag produces hundreds of points, and keeping them all would give a path impossible to
edit and heavy to save. Simplification does not lose the turns, which is the only thing that
matters: that is what the test measures.

**The handles of a smooth node move together**: symmetric mirrors them, smooth keeps their
length and aligns the direction, corner leaves them independent. Moving the node carries the
handles with it, otherwise the curve would deform at every move.

**The shape renderer was generalised**: before it accepted only a `ShapeObject`, now it
receives outline, style and transform, so a free path inherits **for free** gradients,
hatches, shadow, glow and bevel — and print and PDF with them. It was the way not to have two
renderers diverging.

**A defect of mine, found by the log and not by the tests**: the Enter that confirms the command in the
palette **also reaches the grid**, and there it immediately concluded the freshly chosen tool — the
drawing seemed "not working" without any error. Now Enter concludes only if a path is
really in progress, and Escape cancels it. In the same pass: pending points are now cleared on
tool change, instead of resurfacing in the next drawing.

**The ODF trap**: we write `draw:path` with `svg:d`, but **the reference suite rewrites a closed path
of straight lines only as `draw:polygon`** with `draw:points`. Reading only `draw:path` the polygon
vanished on the way back. Now `draw:polygon` and `draw:polyline` are read too.
**Verified with the real reference suite both ways**: four-node polygon and curve with handles,
written by us, converted and read back, come back whole.

**A path's appearance is changed from its dialog**: `ShapeStyleView` no longer works on a
`ShapeObject` but on **outline plus style** (`StyledOutline`), so the same dialog dresses
preset shapes and free paths. It was the way not to have two style dialogs.

**The path was drawn at the sheet's corner** instead of where it had been traced: the
selection box was right, the drawing was not. The transform I passed to the renderer
contained only the rotation, and **the translation to the box was missing** — the outline is scaled
relative to the origin, so without translation it ends up at the grid's origin. Reported
by the user looking at the screen, which is the only place where a position defect is seen.

In the same pass the free path was added to **printing**, where it did not exist: the
choice of colours from the style is now a single function, shared with shapes, instead of a
second copy bound to diverge.

### Form controls: real properties and events (done)
Three defects reported while looking at the application, and all three were symptoms of something
bigger.

**A deselected control could no longer be selected.** Outside design mode the click goes *to the
control*, so it also swallowed clicks on things that do not react — a label, a group frame. Now the
click goes to the control **only if that control responds**, the right button always selects the
object under the pointer (it was needed for the context menu anyway), and ⌥+click also selects what
responds.

**The properties were few and the same for everyone.** Now the catalog declares for each type the
**property groups** that belong to it (text, number, date, list, image, button, scroll) and the
**events** it can raise, and the dialog is built from there: four tabs — General, Data, Appearance,
Events — with fields that really change according to the control. The model grew accordingly: font
and colors, border, alignment, maximum length, password character, multiline, decimals and thousands
separator, currency symbol, bound column, drop-down rows, button action and URL, bar orientation,
help text.

**Events hook real macros.** The document now has a **macro library** (`Workbook.Macros`: name,
language, source), and a control binds an event to a macro name. `FormEventRunner` runs it in the
right engine, in the sandbox, with the sheet and the control name among the global variables; an
*Approve* event that returns false stops the change. A macro that is referenced but missing does not
bring anything down: it ends up in the log.

In ODF the hooks are `office:event-listeners` with `script:event-listener`, and the macros live in
`Scripts/pulseoffice/` with their index. Non-standard properties go through `form:properties`, as
already decided for the linked cell.

**The fields panel was extracted** (`FormFieldsPanel`) because it was needed inside the tabs and not
only as a whole dialog: without it, the tabbed dialog would have had a second construction of the
fields, that is a second place in which to fix them.

### Form controls (done)
Coverage from 233 to **259 commands out of 373 (69.4%)**.
Twenty-one controls — label, text box, check box, option button, list box, combo box, push button,
formatted fields, group frame, image control, file selection, table control, navigation bar, spin
button, scroll bar — with properties, activation order, cell binding and saving in ODF.

**A control is an `EmbeddedObject`**, like charts and shapes: so it is born already fit for Folio and
Deck, and anchors to a cell like everything else. The model (`PulseOffice.Document/Forms`) does not
know Avalonia, so catalog, tab order and interaction are tested without UI — and they are tested.

**Controls are drawn, not hosted.** A layer of real controls above the grid would have meant a second
implementation of zoom, scrolling and frozen panes; drawing them with the same `DrawingContext` as
everything else makes them exist in print and PDF too.

**Cell binding follows the spreadsheet convention**: a check box writes TRUE or FALSE, a list writes
the **one-based position**, a bar writes the number, the rest writes the text. A value coming from
the cell is brought back inside the control's range instead of being rejected.

**Outside design mode the click acts on the control**, it does not select it: the check box turns on,
the list picks the row under the pointer, the bar is dragged. Every change goes through the history,
so ⌘Z undoes both the control and the linked cell.

**The ODF trap, found only by testing with the real reference suite.** The controls disappeared on
opening: the form came back empty and the frames remained orphaned. The cause was not in the
attributes but in a **namespace prefix**: `form:control-implementation` holds
the vendor-qualified control type name, which the reference suite resolves as a **QName**, not as
a string. Without `xmlns:ooo` declared the service name does not resolve, the creation of the control
fails and the element is discarded **silently**. With the prefix declared, everything comes back.
Two shape corrections were also needed: the non-standard settings (linked cell, source range, group,
bar bounds) go in `form:properties` and not in invented attributes, and the group frame is
`form:frame`, the bar is `form:value-range`.

**Verified with the real reference suite in both directions**: check box with label and linked cell,
list with three entries, push button — written by us, converted by the reference suite and read back,
they come back whole.

### Names that end up on disk are in English
The files in the configuration folder and the settings keys were in Italian (`impostazioni.json`,
`aspetto.tema`). They are names that live **in the files**, not in the interface, and so the same rule
already in force for formulas, format codes and log messages applies: canonical English form in what
is written, translation only at display time. The titles stay translated into the five languages,
because the translation keys are **derived** from the setting key and changed with it.

`impostazioni.json` → `settings.json`, `recenti.json` → `recent.json`,
`finestra.json` → `window.json`, `connessioni.json` → `connections.json`,
`ripristino/` → `recovery/`, `raccolte/` → `libraries/`.

There is no conversion from the old names: anyone who already had files starts again from the factory
preferences. Writing it would have meant keeping forever a piece of code that serves only once, and
preferences can be set again in a minute — documents, which are what matters, are touched by nobody.

### The window remembers where it was, and knows how to become visible again
Position, size and maximized state are kept between one session and the next. They live in their own
file (`window.json`) and not among the settings, for the same reason as recent documents: they change
at every close, and mixing them with the preferences would mean rewriting the preferences every time.
Writing is atomic and a corrupted file does not prevent startup.

The part that matters is not remembering, it is **remembering without making the window disappear**: a
disconnected screen, a changed resolution or a switched-off monitor leave a position that no longer
exists, and a window restored there cannot be seen or reached. `PlacementPolicy` is therefore pure
logic, without Avalonia and tested: it chooses the screen on which the window fell the most, reduces
the size to that of the screen, and **brings back inside** whatever sticks out. If less than 40 percent
remains visible, the position is not corrected: the window is re-centered, because a window shrunk into
a corner is as much a defect as an invisible one.

A size below the minimum or a non-finite coordinate are not corrected but **discarded**: they are the
sign of a badly written file, not of a user choice, and the window starts again from the default
values, centered.

The two units do not mix: screens and position arrive in physical pixels, size in density-independent
points. The conversion goes through the screen's scale factor, because on a double-density panel
confusing them would give a window twice or half as large.

### The ribbon flyout menu had no shadow
A panel floating above the sheet without a shadow does not read as something that sits *above*: it
looks like a rectangle glued to the page. The shadow on the internal template of the `FlyoutPresenter`
was not enough, because the popup clips its own content and the shadow remained outside the clip.

The solution is to give the shadow **the space in which to exist**: the content is a surface with its
own margin, and the presenter hosting it becomes transparent (class `plain`, with the `PopupRoot`
transparent in turn). The shadow is therefore drawn inside the popup, not at its edges. Soft radius and
border line follow the tokens, like the other floating surfaces.

### Closing with unsaved changes: now it asks
The application closed **without saying anything** even with a modified sheet. Autosave put aside a
recovery copy, so the work did not vanish entirely — but a clean exit **discarded** the copies, because
by definition what remains there is what a crash left behind. Closing on purpose was therefore the
quickest way to lose everything.

`IUnsavedChangesGuard` lives in the **shell** and not in Ledger, because the question is the same for
the three modules; saving, instead, is specific, so it goes through `IDocumentSaver` — today only
Ledger implements it, and the guard chooses whoever knows how to save that document. The three answers
are the usual ones: **Save**, **Don't Save**, **Cancel**.

The delicate point is the **order**: the dialog is an internal modal and therefore asynchronous, while
the close request is synchronous. The close is therefore **cancelled immediately**, the question is
asked, and only after a favorable answer is the window really closed — with a flag that prevents the
second close from asking again. It applies both to the window and to ⌘Q, and also to the ✕ of a single
tab: there only that document is considered.

**All three paths verified live**: with 42 written in D2, ⌘Q shows «Ledger1 ha modifiche non salvate»
(Ledger1 has unsaved changes); *Cancel* leaves the application open, *Don't Save* closes it, *Save*
opens the save dialog, writes `Ledger1.ods` and **then** closes.

### The typed value ended up in the wrong cell
Typing in a cell and **clicking on another**, the value appeared in the clicked one. It is the most
serious defect a spreadsheet can have — it writes where the user is not looking — and it arose from an
order of events:

the click **first** moves the selection, and only afterwards does the selection change commit the
edit in progress. The commit wrote into `_selection.Active`, which at that point was already the new
cell.

The fix is the principle, not the patch: **the edit remembers its own cell**. When the editor opens,
the address is noted, and the commit writes there — just as protection and validation are checked
there, which before also looked at the wrong cell and would have let through a value rejected by the
original cell.

**Verified live**: `123` written in D2 and click on H5 → 123 stays in D2 and the selection goes to H5;
`=1+1` written in D3 and click on I8 → D3 shows 2.

### A ribbon group's menu scrolled horizontally
The *Cells* group hid eleven commands, and their menu laid them out **in columns of three rows** — the
same rule as the open group. Eleven commands became four columns, the menu went outside the window and
a horizontal scroll bar appeared, with the last column cut in half.

The rule of the open group does not apply to its menu: there the scarce space is **the ribbon height**,
here it is **the screen width**. Now the menu chooses the rows so as not to exceed three columns, and
if even so it becomes too tall it scrolls **vertically**. A menu that scrolls sideways hides commands
without saying they exist — it is the same reason why ribbon groups collapse instead of scrolling the
bar.

**Verified on screen**: the eleven hidden commands of *Cells* now fit in three columns of four rows,
inside the window and with nothing cut.

### The context menu had become a list: now it has submenus
As commands were added, the cell menu had reached forty entries in a single column as tall as the
screen. Group labels were no longer enough: they say *where* you are, they do not reduce what you read.

Two changes, one of rendering and one of structure:
- `CommandSurfaceFactory` builds **real submenus**: a node that has children instead of a command
  becomes an entry with an arrow, and the group's leaves stay at the top. Before, construction stopped
  at the second level and the grandchildren disappeared;
- the command paths were **reorganized into three levels** (`cell/cells/rows`, `cell/format/align`,
  …). This is not a presentation detail: the path is the only thing that decides where a command
  appears, so the menu hierarchy **is** the path hierarchy.

The result: five short groups — Clipboard, Cells, External data, Format, Comments — with four
submenus (Rows, Columns, Fill, Insert and delete) and two under Format (Alignment, Case). Twenty rows
instead of forty.

**Two defects fixed in the same round:**
- **Exiting the application threw an exception**: the DI container now contains a service that
  implements only `IAsyncDisposable` (the IronPython engine), and `Dispose()` on a `ServiceProvider`
  that contains one **throws** instead of ignoring it. Shutdown now goes through `DisposeAsync`, which
  is the only correct one for a container hosting asynchronous services.
- **The real-server tests were no longer skipped**: `TcpClient.ConnectAsync(...).Wait(...)` wraps the
  error in an `AggregateException`, which the `catch (SocketException)` did not catch. With the
  containers stopped, the check that was meant to *skip* the test made it fail. Now they are really
  skipped: 31 tests ignored and no red.

### B14-B20 — Sparklines, data areas, revisions, macros (done)
Coverage from 204 to 233 commands out of 373 (62.5%). The new pieces:

**Sparklines**: they are not anchored objects, they are **cell properties**, and the grid draws them
together with the content. A group shares type, colors and — if requested — **the scale**, because it
is the comparison between neighboring cells that makes a column of charts readable. They are saved in
ODF as `calcext:sparkline-groups`. **Verified live**: 3, 8, 5, 9 in a row become four columns in a
single cell.

**Named data areas** (`DatabaseRange`): define, select, refresh. It is the form that Excel calls a
"table" and the reference suite calls a "database range".

**Revisions**: `ChangeLog` records who changed what, when, from which value and with which formula.
Recording **is switched on**, it is not always active: a log that grows by itself is a file that swells
without anyone having asked for it. Modified cells have a purple border, and rejecting a change **puts
back the previous value by going through the engine** — and disables recording while doing so,
otherwise the rejection would generate a change to be rejected.

**Macros, for real**: there was only the abstraction. Now there are two engines — Jint for JavaScript
(already written but not connected) and **IronPython**, new — plus an editor with execution, output
and diagnostics, and the sheet exposed to the script as an object `foglio` with `Read`, `Number`,
`Write`, `SheetName`, `Selection`. Execution **in the sandbox** with time and memory caps.

Three defects found while doing it, all instructive:
- **Jint throws `TimeoutException`**, not `ExecutionCanceledException`, when `TimeoutInterval`
  expires: without that `catch` an infinite loop brought the application down instead of stopping;
- **IronPython writes output in UTF-16** when it runs inside the test runner, and in UTF-8 when it runs
  on its own. Now the text is decoded **by looking at the bytes** (preambles and zeros in odd
  positions), instead of trusting the declared encoding;
- **a macro writes from a background thread**: the first `foglio.Write` brought the application down
  with "the calling thread cannot access this object". The right boundary is the facade: it is the one
  that carries writes onto the UI thread, and the engines remain unaware of the existence of a window.

Also added: preset zooms, the toggles for formula bar, tabs, headers and full screen, and save a copy,
save all, reload.

**What remains (135 commands)**, by group: forms and controls (33), interactive drawing and galleries
(21), minor insertions such as symbols and fontwork (12), view and page (10), spelling and language
(8), digital signature (4), and 47 scattered entries. The three big families — form controls, freehand
drawing tools, spelling with dictionaries — are subsystems, not commands: each is worth a block of its
own, and they must be tackled as such instead of piecemeal.

### B7-B13 — The big dialogs, names, view, calculation (done)
Coverage went from 152 to 204 commands out of 373. The pieces that matter:

**`TabbedDialogView`**: the framework for tabbed dialogs, which `FormPromptView` could not be — it was
born for five fields. Tabs build their own content **the first time they are opened**, so a dialog with
six tabs does not pay for six constructions to show one.

**Format Cells** (six tabs: numbers, font, alignment, borders, background, protection) and **Insert
Function** (categories, search, signature, arguments, formula preview). They are the two dialogs that
make the work already done visible: the 534 functions existed and there was no place to discover them.

**Defined names**: the model had them and the engine already resolved them in formulas; what was
missing were the dialogs and **saving in ODF**. Now `table:named-range` for ranges and
`table:named-expression` for constants; in XLSX they were already there.

**View**: show formulas, show grid, value highlighting. And **print preview**, which is not a new view:
`IPageCanvas` existed for PDF, and `AvaloniaPageCanvas` paints it on screen. The same pagination, two
surfaces — if they were two drawings, they would be two sets of defects.

**Manual calculation** (F9, hard recalculation, autocalculate, formula to value): the switch lives in
the engine, and with it off `RecalculateFrom` only marks that there is work to do.

**Cells with shifting**: inserting and deleting cells pushing right or down. A rule that is noticed only
if it is wrong: **a formula that moves does not change its own references**. It moves the container,
not what it points to. Limit declared: references *to other moved cells* are not rewritten, and a
partial rewrite like the one for rows will be needed.

**AutoInput** (`AutoInput`): pure, tested logic — it completes only if the prefix identifies **a single**
value in the column, and numbers and formulas are never completed. Verified live: "Mi" under Milano and
Torino becomes Milano.

And the dialogs that were missing for things already written: consolidation, multiple operations,
advanced filter. With them **B6 is closed**, and with it the habit of stopping at the engine.

### B3-B6 — Images, properties, everyday gestures, filters (done)
Four blocks of the [completion plan](docs/completion-plan.md), which brought the coverage of the
reference suite's spreadsheet commands from 117 to 152 out of 373.

**Raster images**: `RasterImageObject` existed in the model and nobody used it. Now they are inserted
from file, drawn in the grid, saved in ODF (`Pictures/` with the manifest entry) and in OOXML
(`ImagePart` plus `xdr:pic`), and they have their commands — original size, fit to cell, replace,
save, crop, alternative text. **The original bytes are never re-encoded**: recompressing a JPEG at
every save wears it out.

**Document properties**: before, they were discarded, so opening and re-saving someone else's file
erased its author. Now they live in `PulseOffice.Document.Metadata` and cross `meta.xml` in ODF and
`docProps` in OOXML, with the dialog to edit them; on save the modification date and the save counter
update themselves.

**Everyday gestures**: directional fills (⌘D and its three siblings), paste special with
**transposition, arithmetic operations and skip blanks**, clear formatting, exact row height and column
width, hide and show rows and columns, selections (row, column, data area, array), F4 for the
reference type, repeat the last operation.

Three decisions inside these commands:
- **hiding remembers the size**: `SheetLayout` keeps the manually set height, because otherwise
  showing again would return a standard row and the work of whoever had sized it would be lost;
- **F4 is pure, tested logic** (`ReferenceCycler`): A1 → $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 → A1, on the reference
  under the cursor;
- **"repeat" is not "re-run the command"**, it is re-run *on the current selection*: the executor
  remembers the last repeatable command, and the list of those that are not (undo, redo, palette) is
  explicit.

**AutoFilter from the interface**, which was the most glaring gap: the engine was written and tested,
and there was no way to apply it. Now `AutoFilterState` is sheet data, the grid draws the drop-down
button in the headers (green when that column filters), and the menu shows the distinct values with
check marks plus a free condition. Hiding remains a fact of the view: the model says **which rows do
not pass**, and this has not changed.

**Defect found by the live test, not by the tests**: the *Repeat* command asked for a
`Func<CommandExecutor>` that was not registered in the container, and **the application no longer
started**. The tests do not compose it; only the real startup does. It is the second time this has
happened, and the remedy is not remembering it: it is that every block ends with the application open
in front of you.

### B2 — CSV and delimited text (done)
`PulseOffice.Formats.Interchange` is no longer a placeholder. The parser lives in
`PulseOffice.Foundation/Text/DelimitedText.cs` because it serves two masters: the CSV reader and
**Text to Columns**, which had its own copy of the same code. Now the copy is gone: `TextToColumns`
delegates, and quotes behave the same way in both places — if they diverged, the same file would give
different results depending on how it is opened.

The real difference between the two uses is that CSV **is not made of lines**: a line break inside
quotes is content, not end of line. The reader therefore works on a stream of characters and not on
`ReadLine`.

**Separator and locale are guessed from the content** (`CsvSniffer`): the separator by counting the
candidates outside quotes, the locale by trying to read the numeric fields with each and keeping the
one that interprets the most, with a bonus for whoever actually uses the decimal separator. On a tie
nothing is chosen: the declared one stays. Without this, `1.250,50` read the English way becomes 1.25 —
a file that opens, looks right and has the wrong numbers, which is the worst damage.

Two more reading rules: **leading zeros stay text** (`007` is a code, not seven), and an empty field
does not shift the columns.

On writing, what needs protecting is protected (separator, quotes, line breaks) and the losses are
declared in `CheckFidelity`: a single sheet, formulas as result, no formatting, no objects or merged
cells.

**Verified live**: a real Italian CSV — semicolon, `1.250,50`, and a field `"Rossi; Ada"` with the
separator inside the quotes — opened by the application gives three columns, the number 1250,5
right-aligned and the whole name in a single cell.

### B1 — Merged cells (done)
`MergedRegions` is sheet data and pure logic: which region covers a cell, which is the anchor, and
**selection expansion** — merging B2:C3 having selected a region that touches it merges the whole
rectangle, and the expansion is repeated until it finds nothing more, because the first growth can
touch regions that the initial selection did not touch.

**Covered cells stay in the model with their content.** Unmerging brings back what was there: deleting
it would be a silent loss, and it is also what the two formats do.

Along this road a defect **worse** than the one being closed was found: the ODF reader scanned only
the `table:table-cell` elements and **skipped the `covered-table-cell`s**, so in someone else's file
with merged cells all the cells to the right of the merge ended up in the wrong column. The merge was
not lost: the data were shifted. Now covered cells are read like the others — they carry the hidden
content — and they also serve to keep count of the columns.

Drawing treats the region as a single cell: the anchor is drawn on the whole rectangle, the covered ones
draw nothing, not even the grid lines. Clicking on a covered cell **selects the anchor**, and the
selection that commands see is the one expanded to the merges, otherwise formatting applied to half a
merge would format cells that cannot be seen.

**Verified with the real reference suite in both directions and both formats**: `A1:C1` and `A4:A6`
written by us, converted by the reference suite and read back come back identical, with the columns in
their place. **Verified live**: text in D2, selection D2:H2, *Format ▸ Merge cells ▸ Merge and center*,
the region is drawn as a single cell with the text centered, clicking on F2 selects D2, and ⌘Z brings
back the separate cells.

### Comparison with the reference suite redone on its source (done)
The functions are complete (534 of 535), and this had given the impression that the rest was too. It
is not. The survey was redone on the **real menu of the reference suite's spreadsheet**, plus its
command labels, which is the most honest definition of functionality because it is what the user can
reach: **426 commands**, of which 119 done, 21 partial and 286 missing. The full count, area by area,
was in a former survey document.

The number matters less than three gaps that on their own are worth more than a hundred entries:
- **merged cells do not exist**, neither in the model nor in the readers: someone else's sheet with a
  merged title at the top loses the merge on opening and forever on saving. It is the only defect that
  **destroys data without saying so**, and it goes ahead of everything;
- **no textual exchange format**: `PulseOffice.Formats.Interchange` contains a single placeholder.
  Without CSV the suite does not talk to the rest of the world;
- **no raster image**: only SVGs are inserted, and those in other people's files are lost. We need it
  too, because OOXML demands a raster thumbnail next to the SVG.

A gap of a different nature, and instructive: **filters can only be removed, not applied.** The engine
is written and tested — standard and advanced filter — but no command applies it and the headers have
no drop-down button. It is the distance between what the project can do and what the user can do, and
it repeats elsewhere: statistical procedures, consolidation and multiple operations are in the same
state or nearly. The missing work is not always engine: often it is **the road to get there**.

**The plan to have them all** is in [docs/completion-plan.md](docs/completion-plan.md): twenty-two
blocks ordered by damage avoided, then by real use, then by what unlocks the rest. Completeness is
**measured, not promised**: a survey script regenerated the map from the reference suite's source,
printed the coverage (today 117 of 373 wanted commands) and **failed if the map cited one of our
commands that no longer exists** — so it could not become a lie while the code changed underneath.

### Structure keys are now watched like titles
The context menu showed `⟦CONTEXT.CELL.DATA⟧`: the new external data group did not have its own
translation. The marker did its job, but **the startup check did not**: it looked only at command
titles, not at the keys of menu, ribbon and context menu groups. Those were exactly the ones missing,
so the hole reached the user instead of the log.

Now `CommandRegistry.StructureKeys()` composes the keys **with the same rule** with which the tree
builder composes them — if they diverged, the check would watch keys that nobody uses — and startup
reports those without translation. Searching for them also turned up the four roots (`context.cell`,
`context.column`, `context.row`, `context.sheet`), which today are not visible because the menu starts
from the groups, but which would have appeared as markers the day the root was shown.

### Dependency arrows (done)
`DependencyTracer` answers three questions about the graph that the engine already maintains: where
this value comes from, who uses it, and where this error originates. The third climbs the chain up to
the origin, skipping healthy cells: it is the only one of the three that really saves time.

The arrows are sheet data and the grid draws them: dot on the origin, arrowhead on the destination,
color by type (precedents blue, dependents green, error red). **Verified on screen** with
`=SUM(A1:A3)`: three arrows from the three cells to the formula.

### Three defects reported by the user, fixed
**1. `HitTest` selected.** Moving the pointer over a column header, the column selected itself: the
method that *queries* where the pointer is **also changed the selection**, and it was also called by
mouse movement (for comment tooltips and for the cursor shape). Now `HitTest` returns a `GridHit` —
corner, row header, column header or cell — and selection happens only on press. A function that
answers a question must not change state: if it does, it is enough to call it for another reason and
the defect appears far from where it was written.

**2. No context menu.** The right button did nothing. Now the menu is a **projection of the command
registry** like the ribbon and the menus: a command declares in which context menus to appear
(`ContextPaths`) and appears there without dedicated code. The menu differs depending on where you
press: on the cell there are clipboard, rows **and** columns, comments and validation; on the column
header only columns. If you press outside the selection, the selection moves before opening the menu —
otherwise the command would act on cells the user is not looking at.

**3. The system menu was in disorder.** Two causes: the paths of some commands used the **dot instead
of the slash** (`view.freeze` instead of `view/freeze`), so "Freeze panes" and "Zoom" became top-level
entries instead of ending up inside *View*; and the top-level menus came out in the order in which the
commands had been declared, that is the order in which the classes were written. Now the order is the
canonical one — File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Sheet, Data, Tools, Help — and it also applies to
the ribbon tabs.

**Verified live**: menu bar in the right order, *View* contains "Freeze panes" and "Zoom", hovering
over the header no longer selects, and the right button opens the right menu on cell and on header. To
test it `uiprobe` can now also do a **right click**.

### Cell styles as document objects (done)
Styles are no longer just values shared by index: the document has a **catalog of named styles**
(`NamedStyleCatalog`) with the twelve basic ones — Default, Heading 1 and 2, Good, Bad, Neutral,
Error, Warning, Footnote, Note, Result — applicable to the selection and creatable from the formatting
of the active cell.

A style can **inherit** from another: `Heading 2` declares only what changes compared to `Heading`,
and the rest comes from the parent. It is the way the formats save them, and it is also why a change
to the parent propagates.

Named styles **are saved in ODF** in `styles.xml`, where the reference suite shows them in its own
gallery. The per-cell link remains to be done — today applying a style copies its formatting, so the
appearance survives but the *name* does not stay attached to the cell.

Two tests said "two styles in the catalog" to verify that equal cells share one: they measured an
absolute number instead of the invariant. Now they measure what matters — that all cells formatted
together have **the same identifier** and that the operation adds **a single** style — and they no
longer break when the document is born with twelve basic styles.

**One dialog out of two was clipped.** The modal frame imposed `MaxWidth` and the content an equal
`MinWidth`: the content went past the edges and was clipped on the right and left, eating the first
letter of the labels and half of the confirm button. Now the frame decides the width and the content
adapts. It applied to **all** dialogs built with the field forms.

### Page styles and split view (done)
The page model — paper sizes, orientation, margins, headers and footers — **moved up into
`PulseOffice.Foundation`**: it is not printing stuff, it is document geometry, and Folio and Deck need
it too. Now the sheet has a **page style** (`Worksheet.PageStyleName` and `Workbook.PageStyles`) that
printing uses instead of fixed values, and the *Page Setup* dialog edits it. **Verified**: set to
landscape, the exported PDF measures 841×595 points instead of 595×841.

**Long text overflows into the empty cells beside it**, as in any spreadsheet: it stops at the first
occupied cell, and to the right or left according to the alignment. It also applies in print. A number
that does not fit keeps showing `###`, because there truncating would mean showing a wrong figure.

**Split view**: panes now have their own scrolling. Frozen panes and split view are the **same
mechanism** with a single difference — when frozen the pane's scrolling stays at zero — and this
avoided two parallel implementations of the same thing.

The work uncovered **two defects that were already there**:
- the content of **frozen rows disappeared** as soon as you scrolled: the cell drawing always
  subtracted the main scrolling, even while drawing the frozen band, which by definition does not
  scroll. Now each pane receives its own origin;
- **clicking in the frozen bands hit the wrong cell** after a scroll, for the same reason: the point
  lookup used a single origin.

### Scenarios in the formats, and a reading defect found by chance
**Scenarios are saved in ODF**. The format does not model them as we do: a scenario is a **hidden
sheet** containing a `table:scenario` element, and the association with the source sheet is
**positional** — the reference suite rewrites the ranges naming the scenario sheet itself, not the data
sheet. The reader therefore attributes the scenario to the sheet preceding it when the name does not
match a real sheet. **Verified**: written, reopened by the reference suite, read back — the scenario
comes back with its values and does not become an extra sheet.

While looking for why a named style did not survive, a defect of **ours** came out, much more serious:
the reference suite, when a column has a uniform appearance, moves the formatting to the **column's
`table:default-cell-style-name`** instead of repeating it on the cells — and we did not read that
attribute. Any third-party file with a formatted column lost its colors on opening. Now it is read, and
the test that failed before now passes.

On the **per-cell style name** in ODF the conclusion is negative and I write it down so as not to try
again: the reference suite discards automatic styles whose `parent-style-name` is not `Default`, and
also discards those with names outside the `ce<number>` convention. The appearance always survives, the
link to the named style does not. The right place to keep it is OOXML, which has `cellStyleXfs` and
does not depend on the application language. pivot tables, solver, subtotals, data validation,
protection, groupings, print ranges, cell comments, styles as document objects.

### Mathematical formula editor (done)
`PulseOffice.Formulas` is a project of its own and **does not know Avalonia**: tree model (fractions,
roots, superscripts and subscripts, delimiters, functions, large operators, matrices, accents), parser
of the StarMath-style **linear form** (`frac {a} {b}`, `sqrt {x}`, `x^2`, `sum_{i=1}^{n}`,
`matrix {a & b # c & d}`, `%alpha`) and layout (`FormulaLayout`) separate from drawing. The formula is
written in a single place and seen on the grid, in print and in PDF, because the renderer receives
boxes already measured.

**A formula is an `EmbeddedObject`**, like charts and shapes: so it is born already fit for Folio and
Deck and anchors to a cell like everything else. The document keeps the **linear form**, not the tree:
it is what the user wrote, and it is the only form that survives a round trip through the formats
intact.

**The two formats, as the rule demands**:
- **ODF** is the native way: each formula is a **sub-document** in the package
  (`Formula N/content.xml`) in **MathML**, with the `draw:frame`/`draw:object` frame anchored in the
  cell and the manifest entry `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.formula`. The MathML carries at the
  end an `annotation` with the linear form, so on reopening **the written text** is recovered and not a
  reconstruction of it.
- **OOXML** speaks **OMML** (`m:oMath`), but an Excel sheet does not host a formula as a drawn object:
  formulas therefore travel in a custom XML part of the workbook, one per document, each with sheet,
  anchor and size. Our files come back whole; a round trip through Excel does not, and the **loss is
  declared** (`XLSX021`) instead of being kept silent.

`MathParityTests` proves that every formula survives **both** syntaxes, and
`XlsxFormulaRoundTripTests` that it comes back from the XLSX round trip with its anchor.

Two traps found while writing it:
- the namespace `PulseOffice.Math` **shadowed `System.Math`** in all `PulseOffice.*` namespaces: every
  `Math.Round` in the project stopped compiling. Renamed to `PulseOffice.Formulas`;
- `CustomXmlPart` **cannot be appended to a `WorksheetPart`**, only to the workbook; and the `id`
  parameter of `AddNewPart` is the relationship identifier, not a free name.

With the formula, coverage of the reference spreadsheet rises to **374 of 414 (90.3%)**.

### Email and Bluetooth (done)
The reference spreadsheet's five send entries. **We do not send**: composing a message means handing it
to the user's mail program, with its accounts and its rules. An SMTP client inside a spreadsheet would
mean asking the user for server, port and **password** — that is the thing this project keeps out of
documents on principle.

`IMailComposer` lives in `PulseOffice.Platform` with three implementations, one per system, like the
keychain and printing:

| System | Route | Attachments |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | AppleScript to Mail: outgoing message **visible**, never sent | yes |
| Linux | `xdg-email --attach`, which respects the default client | yes |
| Windows | `MAPISendMail` from `mapi32.dll`; if missing, fallback to `mailto:` | yes / no |

**`SupportsAttachments` is declared, not hoped for**: the `mailto:` fallback cannot carry a file, and
an attachment that disappears silently would be worse than a command that says it cannot do it. The
command checks it before exporting.

`IFileSharing` does the same for Bluetooth — Bluetooth File Exchange on macOS, `bluetooth-sendto` on
Linux, `fsquirt` on Windows — and when the tool is not there it says so, instead of doing nothing.

**The document is exported to a temporary file** in the requested format (ODS, XLSX or PDF) and then
attached: sending does not touch the user's file nor the modified state.

`SheetPrintDocumentBuilder` was born here: the construction of the printable document lived inside
`LedgerPrintCommands`, and the PDF attachment would have required one group of commands to call
another. Now it is a service, and printing uses it like everyone.

**Verified**: the script for Mail really compiles (`osacompile`), and on this machine Bluetooth File
Exchange lives in `/System/Applications/Utilities/`, no longer in the historical path inside
`CoreServices` — the first version looked for it there and declared it absent. Not tested by really
opening a message: it would open the user's mail client without them having asked.

Reference spreadsheet coverage: **379 of 414 (91.5%)**.

### Compare, merge, versions (done)
**Comparison is pure logic** (`WorkbookComparer` in `PulseOffice.Sheets`): it takes two documents and
returns differences, it touches nothing. Comparison happens **by sheet name** and not by position —
moving a sheet must not make everything look changed — and on cells and formulas, not on computed
values: two documents with the same `=A1` do not differ because one of them was not recalculated.

The differences **are tracked changes**: they enter the `ChangeLog` that already existed, so they are
seen with the purple border and are accepted or rejected with the revision commands, without a second
interface. `ChangeLog.Import` exists because `Record` **respects `IsRecording`**, and a comparison is
not a recording: whoever compares wants the results even with recording off.

*Compare* shows the differences and lets you decide; *merge* (`WorkbookMerger`) also adds the sheets
that the other document has and we do not.

**Versions live inside the document** (`Workbook.Versions`), as in the reference suite: saving one does
not touch the file on disk, and each is the complete ODS package of that moment. In ODF they end up in
the **`Versions/`** folder with the list `Versions/VersionList.xml` in the namespace
the legacy versions-list namespace — names and attributes taken from the **reference suite's
source**, not invented: the first version used `META-INF/versions.xml` with the manifest namespace,
which does not exist.

**The real lesson, which costs an unreadable document.** With the versions inside, the reference suite
refused to open the file: *source file could not be loaded*, not a warning, a refusal. The cause is not
the `Versions/` folder, reserved to the reference suite, but a package rule I had not respected: **every
ZIP entry must be declared in the manifest**, and an undeclared entry is not ignored — it invalidates
the whole document. Found by bisection, building five packages by hand and asking the reference suite
which ones it opened: undeclared refused, declared opened. A test watches it now, comparing the
archive entries with the manifest.

A trap of the tools, not of the code, which wasted more time than the defect: **an already running
the reference suite makes the next one exit with code 0 without converting anything**. For two rounds I believed
in conversions that had not happened. The right check is the existence of the produced file, not the
exit code.

In OOXML neither versions in the file nor shared revision (withdrawn by Microsoft) exist: the two
losses are declared, `XLSX022` and `XLSX023`.

Reference spreadsheet coverage: **382 of 414 (92.3%)**.

### Asian scripts (done)
Six commands, two different natures, and the difference decides what can be shipped inside the
program.

**Width and kana are algorithmic**, so complete and without any data to install
(`PulseOffice.Text/Scripts`, no dependencies): Latin and katakana switch between half width and full
width, hiragana and katakana convert into each other by code point offset. Two details that are noticed
immediately if missing:
- the **voicing mark merges** with the syllable preceding it (`ｶ` + `ﾞ` → `ガ`, `ﾊ` + `ﾟ` → `パ`) and
  is **recomposed** when going back to narrow: treating it as a character of its own would give text
  that no Japanese person would write;
- the space has its own full form (`U+3000`), which is not the widened Latin space.

**Chinese and Hangul/Hanja are not algorithmic: they are dictionaries.** The reference suite keeps them
in three files (`stc_char.dic`, `stc_word.dic`, `hhc_char.dic`) **compiled into its own binary**, so
they cannot even be found on the system like spelling dictionaries. The same choice already made for
spelling and icon libraries then applies: **we do not ship the tables**, they are installed in
`conversions/` in the configuration folder, in the same format as the reference suite (`碼:码` per
character, `word>word` per word). Without tables the command **says where to install them** instead of
doing nothing.

Conversion replaces **whole words first, then characters**: `万历` is a proper name and becomes `萬曆`,
while `历` alone becomes `歷`. Without precedence to the long word one gets text that looks right and is
wrong in the names.

`SheetTextTransform` was born here: applying a transformation to the text of the selection, skipping
formulas and numbers and recording **a single undo**, lived inside `LedgerTextCommands`. It was needed
by two groups of commands, and it is now a service.

**Verified live**, really writing in the cells: `ｶﾀｶﾅ` → *Full width* → `カタカナ` → *Hiragana* →
`かたかな`; and with a two-line table installed by hand, `万历` → `萬曆`. Without a table the status bar
says the exact path in which to put it.

Reference spreadsheet coverage: **388 of 414 (93.7%)**.

### Data import and function wizard: the same form for all
The last two dialogs of the family were aligned with the others, so the four resemble each other and
whoever learns one knows how to use them all.

**Import data**: on the left the connections (the same rows as the dialog that manages them, name and
provider with their icon), on the right the work column — tables and views, then the query **in
monospace** because it is code, then *Preview* with the headers check box beside it, then the real
preview on a bordered plate. The sections have their small-caps labels like the ribbon groups.

**Insert function**: full-width search at the top, the three columns with their labels (categories,
functions, detail), the **signature on a monospace plate**, the description, the arguments and — at
the bottom — the **formula being composed**, on its plate, which changes while typing. Before it was a
column of bare text where signature, description and result all read the same.

**A real defect, found while testing these dialogs**: `connections.json` wrote the keys to disk **in
Italian** — `nome`, `stringa`, `utente`, `credenziale`. It is exactly what the canonical-form rule
forbids, and it is the same fix already made in its time for the file names (`impostazioni.json` →
`settings.json`). Now it is written in English (`name`, `connectionString`, `user`, `credential`) and
**the old names are still read**: here a migration is really needed, because the file contains the
user's connections, not a preference that can be set again in a minute. Three new tests watch it,
including the one that looks for the password in the saved file.

**Verified live against the same SQLite**: in the import the connection appears on the left, the list
shows the table `articoli` read from the real database, choosing it shows `SELECT * FROM articoli`,
*Preview* shows the row (id 1, name Dado) and *Insert* brings it into the sheet with headers. In the

Redone with the same division as the other: on the left the **connections** (name, provider and

and together read as one thing; the connection string carries an **example as placeholder** instead of
a mute field; and the red warning about the plain-text password appears in its strip only when the

### The remote storage dialog was a command panel, not a browser
Five grey buttons in a row — *Sign in*, *Save the storage*, *Forget*, *Connect*, *Parent folder* — two
drop-down menus, an empty frame and a warning line that never went away. It showed **all the commands
together** instead of showing **the files**, which is what such a dialog is opened for.

Now the body is divided like a file browser: on the left the **storages** (name, service and icon —
cloud for the cloud, server for WebDAV) with *New storage* and *Edit* below; on the right the

right panel becomes a form with labeled fields, and shows **only those that service uses** — WebDAV
asks for address, user and password, the others do not. The *Forget* button appears only when editing
an existing storage, because on a new one there is nothing to forget.

and you have not signed in yet — before it stayed written even after changing service, which is the
quickest way to make nobody read it anymore. The explanation about iCloud was removed from the browser:
whoever chooses iCloud Drive sees their folder, and the limit stays declared by the command, which says

folder — 24 Sep 2026) and «bilancio.ods — 4 kB — 24 set 2026», double click enters *Conti* and the

### Cloud storage: OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox and iCloud (done)
The extension point really existed: each provider is one more implementation of `IRemoteStorage`, and
the five remote commands were not touched. The new project is `PulseOffice.Remote.Cloud`, which does
not know the interface.

**Sign-in is OAuth with PKCE and no application secret.** A program installed on the user's computer
cannot keep a `client_secret`: anyone extracts it from the binary. So the **proof-of-possession** flow
is used (random verifier, SHA-256 challenge) and the response comes back to a **local listener** on
`127.0.0.1` with a port taken on the fly. The browser is the system one, via the `IShellOpener` that
already existed: so the user types the password where they recognize it, and not inside a window of
ours.

**Refresh tokens live in the keychain**, like database and WebDAV passwords, never in `remote.json`;
the access token lives only in memory and renews itself when it expires. A test watches it.

**We do not ship the application identifiers**: they are in `cloud.json` in the configuration folder,
one entry per service (`{"oneDrive": {"clientId": "…"}}`). Registering the application is an act of
whoever distributes the program, not of the program; without that entry the command **says which file
to fill in** instead of failing with a network error. It is the same rule as the spelling dictionaries
and the Asian conversion tables.

**The three services speak three different languages**, and the difference is not cosmetic:

| Service | Addressing | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| OneDrive | **by path** (`/me/drive/root:/cartella:/children`) | Microsoft Graph, the most direct |
| Dropbox | **by path**, but the path travels in a JSON header (`Dropbox-API-Arg`) | the root is requested with the **empty string**, not with `/` |
| Google Drive | **by identifier**: paths do not exist | every folder must be resolved by walking the names from the root, and a new file is first created as metadata and then filled |

**iCloud Drive is declaredly different, and only on macOS**: Apple offers no file API to third-party
programs. The only honest road is the **synced folder**
(`~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs`), so there PulseOffice reads and writes real files
and lets the system sync. The path is found by `ISyncedFolderLocator` in `PulseOffice.Platform` — no
`#if` — and outside macOS the command **says so** instead of showing an empty folder. That is where the
limit is really met, so that is where it must be said: the browser shows the files and that's it.

**Check-out does not exist in the cloud, and it is declared.** WebDAV has `LOCK` per RFC 4918;
OneDrive, Drive and Dropbox do not offer a lock to third-party programs, and a synced folder even less.
The *Check Out*, *Cancel Check-Out* and *Check In* commands are therefore **disabled** on these
connections (`IRemoteStorage.SupportsCheckOut`), and the attempt answers with its own code (`CLOUD030`,
`CLOUD031`) instead of faking a padlock nobody would respect.

**Verified live on iCloud Drive**, in both directions and with this Mac's real folder: 42 written in the
sheet, *Save to remote storage* with iCloud Drive service → the file appears in `com~apple~CloudDocs`;
then *Open from remote storage* lists «Ledger1.ods», opens it in a new tab and the 42 is in its place.
The other three cannot be tested live here — they require a registered identifier and access to a real
account — and are tested against a fake service that answers like theirs: listing, download, upload,
rejected token and Google's name walk.

A defect found by the tests and not by eye: a JSON **valid but not an object** (a list at the top)
brought the three readers down with an exception instead of giving an empty list.

### Remote documents: WebDAV, and check-out is a real lock (done)
Five commands — open, save, check out, cancel, check in — on `PulseOffice.Remote`, a project of its own
that does not know the interface, plus `PulseOffice.Remote.UI` for the dialog that the three
applications will share, as already `PulseOffice.Data.UI`.

**The protocol is WebDAV**, and it is not a fallback choice: it is HTTP, so no native binary and no
`#if`, and Nextcloud, ownCloud, SharePoint and NAS devices speak it. The part that matters is that
**check out and check in are not our invention**: they are RFC 4918's `LOCK` and `UNLOCK`. Checking out
asks for an exclusive lock, checking in uploads the file *with its own token* and then releases it;
whoever writes without a token receives `423 Locked`, which becomes "the document is checked out by
someone else". Without the server's lock, check-out would be a promise made only to the user who sees
it.

**Credentials do not enter the connections file**: `remote.json` carries name, address and user, the
password lives in the system keychain (`ISecretVault`), as is already the case for databases. A test
watches it by serializing the connection and looking for the word "password" in it.

**The downloaded remote document lives in its own temporary folder**, and keeps its own name: the first
version put a GUID in front of the file name and the tab showed `bcaa007bff…-bilancio` instead of
`bilancio`.

**Two defects found live, invisible to the tests:**
- **Entering a folder lost everything.** The addresses WebDAV returns are absolute *on the server*
  (`/dav/conti/`), while ours reattached them to the connection root, which already ends in `/dav`:
  `/dav/dav/conti` was requested and the folder came out empty. Now paths come back **relative to the
  storage root**, which is the only form that does not depend on where the server is mounted.
- The temporary name in the title, mentioned above.

And one that is mine and not the code's: `Uri.TryCreate("/conti/bilancio 2026.ods", UriKind.Absolute)`
**is true on Unix** — an absolute path is a file URI — and `AbsolutePath` returns it re-encoded, so
names came back with `%20` inside. Now only what declares a scheme is parsed as a URI.

**Verified live against a real WebDAV server** (a minimal server written for the test): folder listing,
opening `conti/bilancio.ods` which appears with its 42, check-out announced in the status bar, edit to
99, check-in — and **the file on the server contains 99**. After check-in the check-out command became
available again, that is the lock had really been released. The automated tests do the same round
against an `HttpListener` that speaks PROPFIND, GET, PUT, LOCK and UNLOCK: 17 tests, including the
credentials coming from the keychain and the `423` to whoever writes without a token.

A declared limit: the message of a network that does not answer comes from the system and stays in
English ("Connection refused"), because it is not a text of ours to translate.

Reference spreadsheet coverage: **393 of 414 (94.9%)**.

### Scanner (done)
Two commands — select source, acquire — behind `IScannerService` in `PulseOffice.Platform`, with the
same shape as printing, mail and keychain.

**TWAIN does not exist outside Windows**, so it is not the road: the cross-platform constraint applies
here too. **SANE** (`scanimage`) is used on Linux and macOS and **WIA** on Windows, driven by a
PowerShell script that talks to `WIA.DeviceManager`. macOS has no scanning command of its own: if SANE
is not installed, the command **says so** instead of doing nothing — it is the same rule as the
conversion tables and the dictionaries.

The chosen source, resolution and color are **real settings** (`LedgerSettings`, category *Devices*),
not variables hidden in the command: they can be found in the settings dialog and survive closing, with
translated titles derived from the key as for all the others.

`SheetImageInsertion` was born here: reading the pixel dimensions, deducing the media type and
inserting the anchored object with its undo lived inside `LedgerCommands`. The scanner needed it
identically, and a second copy would have diverged at the first touch-up.

**Verified live in both directions**: without `scanimage` installed the command answers «Nessuno
strumento di acquisizione su questo sistema» (No acquisition tool on this system); with a fake
`scanimage` placed on the path — which lists two scanners and produces a PNG — the dialog shows the two
devices, the resolution and the color, and *Acquire* really inserts the image into the sheet, anchored
to the selection and already selected. There is no real scanner on this machine: what can be tested is
our code, and that is tested.

Reference spreadsheet coverage: **395 of 414 (95.4%)**.

### The last nineteen entries: reference spreadsheet coverage is 414 of 414 (100%)
Nineteen commands in four waves, and three of them were already done and not mapped (second window,
closing the window). What matters is not the number: it is that no entry was closed with a placeholder.

**Opening with the system application** (`IShellOpener`, three roads: `open`, `xdg-open`, Windows
shell) supports three commands — preview in the browser, online dictionaries, edit with an external
tool. The preview goes through a **real HTML writer** (`HtmlSpreadsheetWriter` in
`PulseOffice.Formats.Interchange`), not through string printing: it respects merges, alignments, bold
and colors, and declares its own losses like every other format.

**External editing comes back by itself**: the temporary file is watched (`IExternalEditWatcher`) and
on save the image comes back into the sheet, with its undo. The first version kept the watchers in a
`static List` — a `static` with state, against rule 1: it became a service.

**Objects and media are a `PackagedObject`**: a file kept whole in the document, with its type, drawn as
a plate with the icon (sheet or play triangle) and the name, and openable with the system application.
It is the cross-platform answer to OLE objects, which are COM and therefore Windows: embedding *the
file* works everywhere, and what is lost — editing inside our document — is something not even the
reference suite does outside Windows.

**The image map** lives on the image (`RasterImageObject.Map`) and is pure logic: rectangle, circle and
polygon, with the classic edge crossing for the polygon. Zones are written in 0..1 fractions, so they
stay valid when resizing the image.

**Redaction really replaces the content** — and the dialog says so: ⌘Z brings it back, but nothing of
the original remains in the saved file. It is the only honest form: a graphic cover would leave the data
inside the file, which is how confidential documents get lost.

**A real defect found live**: the IBAN was redacted **halfway** (`AIT60X■■■■56`), because the phone
pattern, applied afterwards, ate a run of digits inside data already recognized. In a redaction a
residual fragment is worse than no redaction. Fixed by **ordering the patterns from most specific to
most generic** and tightening the phone one with word boundaries; seven new tests watch it, one of
which looks precisely for fragments.

**Sharing is a lock file** next to the document (`.~lock.<name>#`), written with `FileMode.CreateNew` —
which is atomic and therefore solves the race between two people opening together. Whoever arrives later
sees user name and machine of whoever holds the lock.

**The side panel really exists**: not a disguised modal, but a region of the shell beside the work area,
with registrable pages (`ISidePanelHost`). The first page is the **named styles**, applicable with one
click.

**Toolbars, interface and customization are real settings and have an effect**: the visibility of
ribbon, status bar and tabs is a setting that the shell follows live, and the *Menu only* mode really
hides the ribbon while *Compact* brings it to two rows instead of three. A switch that moves nothing
would have been worse than an absent command. Customization changes the **shortcuts**
(`CommandRegistry.Rebind`), which is the part of "Customize" that makes sense in a suite with declared
commands.

**XML filters** are a catalog of the user's XSLT stylesheets (`IXmlFilterCatalog`), with real
transformation via `XslCompiledTransform`; the **developer tools** show the real state of the model —
sheets, cells, objects, styles, current cell, history, registered commands.

**Thirteen entries stay out by declared choice**: they are wizards and dialogs specific to the reference
suite that make no sense here. The survey counts them separately and coverage is **413 of 413 (100%)**
on the wanted commands.

### "Organize dialogs" served no purpose: removed
The command opened a dialog titled after dialogs that **listed the macros**, and on a new document it
said «Nessuna macro nel documento» (No macros in the document): the title promised one thing and the
content showed another. The list moreover already existed in the command next to it (*Organize
macros*), so they were two menu entries for the same thing.

In the reference suite that entry is the *Dialogs* tab of the macro organizer: a **Basic form
designer**, where fields and buttons are drawn inside a library of the document. Here there is no Basic
and no form designer — macros are JavaScript and Python and dialogs are built by the program — so it is
not a command to implement but a subsystem to invent, and it is not in the plan.

The real defect was in the **map**, which marked the row as `fatto` (done): coverage counted as closed
an entry that was a placeholder, that is exactly what the survey exists to prevent. Now it is
`escluso (progettista di maschere Basic)` (excluded (Basic form designer)) next to the other twelve, and
the count — 413 of 413 — tells the truth.

### The scriptable API: from twelve members to one hundred thirty
The editor had become an IDE with almost nothing to write inside: the facade exposed **twelve
members**, all about the cell. Now the API is divided into **three objects**, as the model is divided:

| Object | Members | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `app` | 11 | log, status bar, clipboard — **the same in all modules** |
| `doc` | 20 | sheets (add, delete, rename, activate), document properties, defined names, undo and redo, recalculation |
| `sheet` | 48 | cells and ranges, formulas, formats, structure, merges, sorting, find and replace, comments, **charts and shapes** |

**It is not a new wrapper around nothing**: every member goes through the services that already
existed — `ISheetStructure` for rows and columns (so formulas are rewritten), `ISheetMerge`,
`ISheetSort` (whole rows, formulas translated), `ISheetFilter` for distinct values, `ISheetSnapshots`
for undo. Writing a cell goes through the calculation engine, so dependents update; every operation
enters the history, so ⌘Z also undoes what a macro did.

**The cross-app part is really there**: `AddChart` and `AddShape` create `EmbeddedObject`s, the same
objects that will live in Folio and Deck; `app` is deliberately free of everything that smacks of
spreadsheet, so in Folio it will be the same object with the same members. The clipboard goes through
`ISheetClipboardService`, which is already the bridge between modules.

**Everything declared is implemented**: the catalog and the facade are written side by side, and a
documented entry that does not exist would be a lie with the look of documentation. The 116
descriptions — three objects, seventy-nine members, thirty-four parameters — are translated into the
five languages.

The Italian aliases (`applicazione`, `documento`, `foglio`) remain valid in code and do not appear twice
in the list.

**Verified live** with a single JavaScript macro: `WriteRange` writes a three-row table, `SetFormula`
puts `B2*C2` in D2 and D3 (which give 15 and 1), `Bold` and `Background` dress the header,
`ColumnWidth` widens the column, `AddChart` inserts a **real column chart** anchored to F2 showing Dado
10 and Vite 4, and `app.Log` prints document name, number of sheets and number of objects. Three hundred
and twelve milliseconds.

### The main menu: sections instead of submenus, and a map in a single place
In the menu bar **Home** and **Review** appeared after *Help*: two commands carried a **ribbon** path
(`home/clipboard`, `review/changes`) in the **menu** field, and an unknown root ends up at the end.
Fixed, and with them other duplicate paths — `insert/object` next to `insert/objects`, `insert/field`
next to `insert/fields`, `edit/links` next to `data/links`.

But the real defect was structural: **every group became a submenu**, so *File* had twelve submenus and
no visible entry. Now the second level is a **section**: entries are in plain view, separated by a line,
and only from the third level down is a submenu born — it is the way menus that can be used without
learning them are made. It applies both to the native macOS menu (`NativeMenuItemSeparator`) and to the
one we draw on Windows and Linux, where sections also carry the **title** in small caps, like the
ribbon groups.

**The menu layout is a decision, and it lives in a single place** (`PulseMenuLayout`): an ordered list of
rules "identifier or prefix → section", plus the order of the sections for each menu. Before, the
structure was the sum of forty files each declaring a path, and nobody could see it whole; now it reads
on one page. The order of the rules is also the order of the entries inside the section, so "Chart…"
comes before "Delete chart" without a second list to keep aligned.

Long families become submenus by declaring it in the path: *Insert ▸ Shapes*, *▸ Paths*, *▸ Form
controls* — twenty-one controls that before stood in a row inside *Tools*.

**Verified live by reading the real menu bar** with AppleScript, menu by menu: nine entries in canonical
order, *File* in six sections (new, open, save, export, print, document), *Sheet* with the sheet
operations separated from rows and columns, and no foreign root.

### Short sections in plain view, long families in submenus
The previous pass had fixed the order and got the measure wrong: **all submenus removed**, the menus
became lists — *Format* reached **79 entries**, *Sheet* 50, *Insert* 45. A list as long as the screen
is no more readable than twelve empty submenus: they are the two extremes of the same mistake, deciding
the shape of the menu **outside** the menu.

Now the decision is one only and lives in a piece of pure, tested logic (`MenuPlanner`, without
Avalonia): a section **stays in plain view if it is short** (up to five entries) and **becomes a
submenu if it is long**; below three entries it never collapses, because a submenu containing two costs
more than it saves. An overall cap of thirty rows remains as a safety net: if a section were added
without noticing, the menu collapses by itself starting from the widest instead of growing beyond the
screen. Today the cap does not trigger: the per-section limit suffices.

The plan is **computed once and rendered twice**: the native macOS menu and the one drawn for Windows
and Linux read the same list of sections, so they cannot diverge. Before, each decided on its own.

**Every menu command now has its own rule.** Seventy-five commands — font effects, number formats,
borders, alignments, zoom, panes, print ranges, breaks, check out and check in, send by mail — were not
named by the map and fell back on the path declared in their own file, that is they appeared in
sections nobody had ordered. The big families became intended submenus — *Format ▸ Cells ▸ Numbers*,
*▸ Borders*, *Format ▸ Font*, *▸ Alignment*, *▸ Case*, *▸ Asian scripts*, *File ▸ Export ▸ Send*,
*Sheet ▸ Print* — and the remote entries have their section in *File*. The rules now also accept a
prefix with `*`, because `ledger.view.zoom*` is the same family written once instead of eight times.

**A menu command without a rule is a defect, and now it shows**: startup reports it in the log
(`Menu commands with no layout rule`), as it already does for missing titles and structure keys. That
is how the seventy-five were found, and the day one is added the log says so and not the user.

**Verified live by reading the real menu bar**, menu by menu and submenus included: File 21 rows with
*Open…*, *Save* and *Save As…* in plain view, *Format* 18 with the four text families, *Sheet* 18,
*Insert* 22, *Data* 19 — and no report in the log.

### Submenus have sections too
The top-level menus were fine and the **submenus** were not: *View ▸ Show* was a column of ten toggles
without a line, *Zoom* eleven, *Sheet ▸ Sheet* thirteen. The section was something that happened only at
the top, whereas it is a menu rule at every level.

Now the planner produces **blocks** and rendering is **recursive**: a submenu is built with the same plan
as the menu containing it. The block is the missing part — a run of consecutive entries stays together
without lines in between, and a line appears only **between** blocks, otherwise sectioning would have put
a separator between every entry.

**A group that contains other groups is never flattened.** It is the rule that holds up the rest:
flattening it loses its name, and it is the name that says what the entries below are — *Show* and
*Zoom* had vanished as containers and their three sub-groups floated inside *View* without a common
meaning anymore. Only a short group of **entries only** is flattened.

**The order now has a single source.** There were two lists — the rules and a table of the section
order for each menu — and the second applied only to the first level, so nested sections came out in
random order. The table was removed: each node is ordered by the **lowest rank among the commands it
contains**, that is by where its first rule is written. The menu order is therefore the order in which
the map is read, at every depth, and there are no two lists that can diverge.

Sixteen families got their sub-sections: *Show* (bars, grid, guides), *Zoom* (steps, values, fit),
*Sheet* (manage, order, appearance, advanced), *Font* (style, effects, superscript and subscript, size),
*Alignment* (horizontal, vertical, text), *Select* (range, visible cells, sheets), *Audit* (arrows,
options, redaction), and so on.

**A wrong title found along this road**: the command that shows and hides the status bar was called
"Sheet tabs" in all five languages — a toggle that declared it did something else.

**Verified live** by reading the real menus entry by entry: *Show* in three sections, *Zoom* in three,
*Sheet* in four, *Select* in three, *Audit* in three, and no report in the last startup.

### The formula editor became an IDE (done)
