It was a text box with ten buttons in a row and a preview rectangle. Now it is an environment of its own
(`PulseOffice.Formulas.Editor`, a new project like the macro one): **1120×720**, palette divided by
category at the top, colored editor in the center, live preview below, searchable reference on the
right, help and problems row.

**The part that matters is the two-way link between text and drawing**, and to have it something that
was missing was needed: **the parser now records where each node comes from**. Positions are not in the
tree — adding them to the records would change their equality, which the formats use — but in a separate
map (`FormulaSpans`) built by **reference identity**, because two identical subformulas are the same
value and would be the same key. From there:
- moving the cursor highlights in the preview the **narrowest** node containing that position, which is
  the one the user is looking at;
- clicking the preview selects in the text exactly the portion that produced it. The renderer now
  returns the map of drawn rectangles (`RenderMapped`), and among those containing the point the
  smallest is chosen.

**The drawing ignored baselines**, and it showed: `x^2 + y^2` came out with the `+` in mid-air and the
root shorter than its content. The layout already computed them (`MathBox.Baseline`) and the renderer
aligned the children **at the top**. Now each child rests on the parent's baseline — rows, function
arguments, bracketed content, body of large operators, matrix cells. In the same pass: **matrix columns
align** (the column measure is a single function, in `FormulaLayout`, used by measuring and drawing) and
the root stroke covers the whole radicand.

**The palette is a catalog, not a row of buttons**: `FormulaCatalog` is pure data next to the model —
ten categories, one hundred twenty entries among constructs, Greek symbols, relations, sets, arrows,
large operators and functions — and it serves the buttons, the searchable list and the documentation.
Each button inserts the piece **with its placeholders** and leaves the cursor inside.

**The symbol vocabulary lives in a single place** (`FormulaVocabulary`): before, the tables were private
inside the parser, so the palette would have had a second copy to keep aligned. Now parser, catalog,
coloring and diagnostics read the same tables — if one diverged, a symbol would appear in the palette and
not be read in the text.

**Coloring tells roles**, not words: constructs in semibold accent, large operators like them, functions
in blue, symbols in amber, quoted text in red, braces and superscripts in grey because they are
scaffolding. A new color was needed in the palette (`PulseInfo`), because with the accent green the
functions and the constructs were indistinguishable.

**Problems are reported while typing** (`FormulaDiagnostics`, pure and tested logic): unclosed brackets,
mismatched closings, open quotes and words that are neither commands nor known symbols. The first are
errors and show in red; the last is an amber warning, because `dx` is not an error — it is text.

**Verified live in full**: `int_0^1 frac {sin x} {sqrt {1 - x^2}} dx = alpha` is drawn as expected, the
matrix `matrix {alpha & frac {1} {2} # sin x & sqrt {n}}` has aligned columns, clicking the ½ fraction
in the preview the text selects exactly `frac {1} {2}`, and moving the cursor the preview highlights the
corresponding piece. Help opens in the right panel, and the reference shows for each entry **its
drawing**, the form to write and the explanation.

### Ribbon labels were clipped, and it was not the width
«Fuoco automatico sui contr», «Converti la formula in valor», «Togli le frecce dei precede» (truncated
Italian labels: "Automatic control focus", "Convert formula to value", "Remove precedent arrows"): the
text ended up under the next group, **without even the ellipsis** that signals a cut. It was not lack of
space — the window was twice as wide as needed.

The cause is a measuring detail that is noticed only this way: the button content was a **horizontal
stack**, and a stack measures its children with **infinite** width. The text therefore always believed
itself as wide as it wanted and never truncated; the button however had a hand-written cap (176 points)
and what was left over went out of the button, where nobody clipped it and the next group drew over it.
A cap that produces no ellipsis is not a cap: it is an invisible cut.

Now the content is a **grid** (icon at its size, text filling): the text receives a **finite** width and
so really truncates, with the ellipsis, when the cap triggers. The cap rose to 240 points, which is the
measure beyond which a label is no longer a label; large buttons have a declared text width instead of a
maximum, so the line wraps at the right point and the button is born as wide as its content.

**Verified on screen**: the four long labels read whole, and narrowing the window to 1100 points the
ribbon collapses as before — groups reduced to the first commands and then gathered into the group
button — without anything left clipped.

### Disabled, not gone: two axes instead of one (done)
Menus and ribbon were built **by filtering the applicable commands**, so a command that could not be
executed at that moment **disappeared**. The defect is not aesthetic: with a single cell selected *Merge
cells* was not there, with an empty clipboard *Paste* was not there, on a freshly opened document *Undo*
was not there — and whoever looks cannot distinguish "does not exist" from "not now". Menus changed
shape at every click, which is the quickest way to stop learning where things are. A command's place
must be **stable**; grey takes care of saying whether it can be used.

Rendering was already ready (`IsEnabled` on menu items and ribbon buttons): it was always true, because
the tree arrived already filtered. What was missing was the distinction in the model, and now it is
there:

| Axis | Who decides | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Presence** (`IsPresent`) | the module and the opening of a document | the command is there or not |
| **Enablement** (`IsEnabled`) | selection, state, document content | on or off |

`AdditionalCondition` is now called **`EnabledWhen`**, because that is what it does: it no longer hides
anything. Menus and ribbon are built from the **present** commands; the executor rejects a disabled
command anyway, so a shortcut cannot bypass the grey.

**Hiding remains right in two places**, and nothing changed there: the **context menu** — which speaks
about what was pressed on, and a list of grey entries would say nothing useful — and the **contextual
tabs** of the ribbon, which by definition exist only when there is the object
they refer to.

**The analysis of the conditions, command by command, found real faults:**
- **read-only did not really exist.** `DocumentState.ReadOnly` was set by nobody: sixty-six commands
  declared it as a forbidden state and none of them was disabled, and *Edit mode* merely wrote a message
  in the status bar. Now it is a property of the **open document** (`OpenDocument.IsReadOnly`), it enters
  the facts published by the workspace and **cell writing respects it** — otherwise the screen would say
  one thing and the document another;
- **Paste was always enabled**, even with an empty clipboard: only *Paste special* checked. Now the whole
  family asks for `HasContent`;
- **Cut, insertion and deletion of rows and columns, and the two style commands** did not declare
  read-only among the forbidden states: in a protected document they stayed enabled;
- **Delete chart** was always enabled and did nothing if the selection contained no objects; **Remove
  filter** was enabled without filters; **page breaks**, the **comment** commands and **outline** were
  disabled only after trying. Now they say so beforehand.

**Verified live**, reading the real menus and the ribbon: on a new document *Undo* is grey and turns
black after the first write; with a single cell *Merge and center* is grey and lights up selecting
A1:C1, while *Unmerge cells* stays grey because there is nothing to unmerge; with an empty clipboard the
three *Paste* are grey and *Cut* and *Copy* are not; with no objects selected the **Arrange** group of
*Layout* is all grey but **is there**; and in *Edit mode* the text «vietato» (forbidden) does not enter
the cell, the status bar says «Il documento è in sola lettura» (The document is read-only) and Home
stays enabled only on *Copy* and *Find and replace*.

### Every ribbon command has its icon (done)
With eight full tabs, buttons without icons were no longer a detail: a ribbon of words only reads like a
list, and the width of the buttons becomes that of the text. There were one hundred twenty icons, almost
all for the commands written first; **two hundred six** were missing out of the three hundred one that
the map puts on the ribbon.

All drawn, on the same 24×24 grid and with the same stroke width as the others — **not taken from an
icon font**, for the usual reason: an installed font may be missing.

**The catalog was split** instead of becoming a dictionary of three hundred fifty lines:
`DictionaryIconCatalog` carries the behavior and eight catalogs carry the data per area — cells, data,
formulas, drawing, view, review, tools, page — summed by the `CompositeIconCatalog` that already existed
for shapes. Adding an area is a file, not a change to everyone's file.

**Startup reports ribbon commands without an icon**, as it already does for titles, structure keys and
layout rules. It is the way this project keeps things aligned: the day a command is added to the ribbon,
the missing icon is reported by the log and not by the user. Today the count is zero.

Two defects found by the new tests, both invisible to the eye: two keys had **two drawings** (an alias to
the generic icon and a dedicated drawing, with the alias winning and the good drawing never shown), and
a path went outside the grid. The tests now watch that a key lives in a single catalog, that every path
starts with a move and that **absolute** points stay inside the box — relative commands legitimately
have negative numbers, and confusing them was the first way the test went wrong.

**Verified on screen**, tab by tab: Home with clipboard, font (superscript and subscript included),
alignment and numbers all illustrated; Data with distinct funnels for the three filters; Formulas with
the precedent and dependent arrows; Tools with macros, forms and settings.

### The ribbon had four tabs because nobody had designed it
Out of 437 commands, **thirty-nine** declared a `RibbonPath`: they were the first written, and since then
every new command was born without one. The tabs were four — Home, Insert, Data, Review, plus a View with
two entries — not by choice, but because no other command said where to go. The menus had already
received the right treatment (a map in a single place); the ribbon had stayed behind with the old method,
forty-two files each declaring a path.

**The mechanism was already written, but it could only talk about menus.** `IMenuLayout` became
`ICommandLayout` and the registry now keeps **one map per surface**: same rules, same ordering by rank,
same nesting. The ribbon is not a special case — it is the second surface using the same framework, and
what is fixed for one applies to the other.

An intended difference between the two: **in the menu every command must appear** (a command without a
rule is a defect and the log reports it), while **in the ribbon not** — a ribbon is a selection of what
is used often, and the rest lives in the menus and in the palette. So a command without a ribbon rule
**leaves** the ribbon, instead of appearing wherever it happens: the map is the only source, and the
thirty-nine `RibbonPath`s scattered in the files were removed.

**Eight tabs** (`PulseRibbonLayout`), thirty-eight groups, about **two hundred commands**: Home
(clipboard, font, alignment, numbers, styles, cells, editing), Insert (tables, charts, images, shapes,
drawing, text, objects, controls), Layout (page, breaks, sheet, arrange), Formulas (functions, names,
auditing, calculation), Data (external data, sort and filter, tools, outline, analysis), Review
(proofing, comments, changes, protection), View (views, show, zoom, panes, sheets), Tools (macros, forms,
settings).

**The guard now works both ways**: besides commands without a rule, startup reports **rules that match no
command** — that is, typos. It reports only exact rules, because a prefix that today matches nothing is a
net for tomorrow's commands, not an error. It found twelve in the menu map, among which a real one: recent
documents were named `ledger.file.recent` while they are born as `shell.file.recent.N`, so the rule did
not match them and the recent list ended up outside the section designed for it.

**Verified live**, tab by tab: eight tabs in the map's order, *Home* with seven full groups, *Data* with
"Manage connections", the three filters, validation, consolidate, outline and analysis, *Formulas* with
wizard, names, dependency arrows and calculation, *Review* with spelling, comments, revisions and
protection — and no report in the log at startup.

### Print preview was a postage stamp
The page was drawn in a **fixed 320×420-point** box inside a 420-wide dialog: an A4 reduced to an eighth,
where the text was a grey smudge and the preview previewed nothing. A hand-written size can follow
neither the window nor the paper.

Now the page **measures itself**: `MeasureOverride` returns the scaled sheet size, and the scale comes
from the chosen mode — *fit*, *fit to width*, or a factor between 50% and 200%. The dialog is
**900×760** and the page occupies all the remaining space; beyond the window size there is scrolling,
which is what makes zoom at 150% useful.

Measuring was not enough: **the dialog grew and the page did not**. Two causes, both structural.
`PreferredHeight` was only a **maximum**, so the frame shrank to the content instead of taking the
requested height; it is now a real height, **clipped to the shell's space** — a window smaller than the
screen no longer produces a modal that overflows. And in *fit* mode the page measured itself inside a
scroll viewer, which offers **infinite** height: there was nothing to fit into, and it fell back on a
fallback value. Now in that mode the page declares no size of its own, it stretches in the frame and the
scale is computed from the space it really has.

**Verified live**: with «Riepilogo» (Summary) and 42 in the sheet, the modal is 1240×900 and the page
occupies the full height of the preview area, centered; *Fit to width* makes it fill the width with
vertical scrolling, and at 150% the header «Documento / Foglio1» (Document / Sheet1) is readable.

### The modal footer, and cancel on the left
Every dialog built its own row of buttons: eleven different places, eleven spacings, eleven possible
orders. Now there is **a single footer** (`DialogFooter`) and the shell gives it a real band — raised
surface and a line above, like the header — so the dialog has a top and a bottom and in between what is
read.

**Cancel is always far left**, the concluding action is on the right, and it is the only order the
footer allows: it is not a convention that each view can reinterpret, it is a rule the object imposes.
The primary button takes the **module accent**, so in Ledger it is green, and it is not the grey of all
the others.

`IDialogFooterOwner` is the only way for the footer to leave the body of the dialog and become a
full-width band: the view declares its footer, `DialogHost` extracts it and puts it in a row of its own.
Eleven views converted — field forms, tabs, choices, text, data import, remote storage, function wizard,
filter menu, print preview, formula editor and macro editor.

**A defect of mine, seen immediately**: I had painted the primary button with `SystemAccentColorBrush`,
which does not exist here — the button stayed white on white, unreadable. The project's accent is called
`PulseAccent`, and it is the one the ribbon and the header already use.

### Field forms: the right rhythm and a single scroll
Labels sat right against the field *preceding* them instead of the one they describe: with four points
of gap between one group and the next and two inside the group, the eye could not group them. Now the
distance between groups is five times that between label and field, which is the only thing that makes
a form read without thinking.

**The check box has no label above it**: its text is its content, as in every interface in the world.
Before, a grey label was seen and below it a bare little square, which is the quickest way to make a form
look like a construction error.

**A single scroll.** The form had its own scrolling area inside a dialog that already scrolls: the result
was a field cut in half, with no visible bar, and two *Page Setup* entries that were never seen. Now the
dialog scrolls and that's it.

The fix is in `FormPromptView`, which is also the body of `FormFieldsPanel`: so it applies to all field
dialogs and to the tabs hosting them.

### The modal header
It was a title resting above the content and a ✕ with no weight: the dialog had no top. Now the header
is a real **band** — raised surface, border line detaching it from the body — topped by the **module
accent line**, the same sign that already distinguishes the active ribbon tab and the headers touched by
the selection. It costs three pixels and tells at a glance where the frame ends and where what must be
read begins.

The frame clips its children, otherwise the accent line would go out of the rounded corners; the ✕ is
round and lights up only on hover, because a close button must not compete with the title.

**The title loses the ellipsis.** "Format cells…" is the right name in the menu, where the three dots
promise that a dialog will open; inside that dialog the promise is already kept and three dots remain
that say nothing.

### The macro editor, refined by looking at it (done)
Six corrections requested while looking at the editor, and the first is a decision, not a touch-up.

**The API is in English, period.** The Italian aliases (`foglio`, `documento`, `applicazione`, `pagina`,
`regole`, `convalida`, `filtro`, `scenari`) were removed: two names for the same thing look like a
kindness and are a cost — they double what there is to learn, split the examples found around and make a
language look translated when it is not. API names live in files and scripts, that is where the
canonical English form rule applies; **the interface** stays in the five languages.

**The documentation is no longer a block of text**: the panel draws the title, the signature on a
monospace plate — member name highlighted, parameters in grey, return type in green — the description
with its line spacing, and the **parameters as a formatted list**, name in amber monospace and
explanation beside it. Without color a signature is a line of noise.

**The documentation pane takes more space than the list** (three fifths against two) and the list has
compact rows: before, entries were twice as tall as needed and twelve names out of one hundred thirty
were visible.

**Help lives in a button**, not in a fixed notice at the top: four short paragraphs — editor,
documentation, language, lists — read once and then gone. At the top a single line remains: which is the
default engine and that API names are English.

**«Output» stays «Output» in Italian too**: it is the word that whoever writes code looks for with their
eyes, and translating it makes it more distant, not clearer.

**Verified live**: `typeof foglio` answers `undefined` and `typeof sheet` answers `object`, that is the
alias is really gone; the signature of `rules.AddCondition` appears colored with its six parameters
described one per line; help opens and scrolls; line numbers are visible and the label below says
Output.

### The distribution DLLs are obfuscated (Release publish)
The code is ours and commercial (Folio, Ledger, Deck): the build that is distributed must be obfuscated.
The tool is **Obfuscar** (MIT, managed, no native binary — consistent with the cross-platform constraint
and with the choice of packages already in use), as a local tool in `.config/dotnet-tools.json`.

**What can be obfuscated without breaking anything is obfuscated, and not an inch more.** PulseOffice
resolves many things **by name at runtime**, and a blind renamer destroys them: JSON serialization by
property name (`recent.json`, `window.json`, `settings.json`, `connections.json`, `remote.json`,
`cloud.json`), control types and the `StyledProperty`s that Avalonia cites in the theme, the translation
keys derived from command identifiers. So:
- **only the non-public implementation** is renamed (`HidePrivateApi`), where nobody from outside looks
  — private and internal methods and fields;
- **the public surface is kept intact** (`KeepPublicApi`), which is what JSON, XAML and dependency
  injection reach by name;
- **no string encryption**: they would be decrypted at runtime at every access, that is real overhead on
  a hot path such as composing `command.<id>.title` keys, and they are also the part that breaks most
  easily. The real gain is renaming, which costs nothing at runtime because the names simply disappear.

**Tied to `publish` in Release, not to build.** The distributed artifact is the publish; the normal
build — even in Release — stays in clear, so the development cycle and debugging are unaffected.
`build/Obfuscate.targets` runs after `Publish`: it lists the produced `PulseOffice*.dll`, writes the
Obfuscar configuration and replaces the obfuscated assemblies in the publish. Only our assemblies enter
the list; third-party packages are not touched (Avalonia comes out with its `StyledProperty`s intact). It
can be disabled with `-p:Obfuscate=false`.

**Verified live on the obfuscated app**, not on the tests: it starts, the language loads (the embedded
JSON keys hold), 434 commands, the ribbon draws with *Home* active; `=2+3` in A1 gives 5 (calculation
engine); a JavaScript macro prints 42 (Jint binds CLR objects **by reflection**, and it is the path that
renaming put most at risk); on closing, `window.json` comes out with correct
`X, Y, Width, Height, Maximized` and a valid `settings.json` (serialization by name intact). In the
assembly, `ShowWelcome`, `FillRecent` and `ApplyVisibility` no longer appear — renamed — while
`RecentDocument` and `LastOpened` do, because they are public.

### The open documents bar no longer disappears when typing in a cell
The bar with the document tabs (`Ledger1 ×`) hid itself when there was only one document —
`DocumentTabsView.Refresh` reset `IsVisible = Documents.Count > 1` at every call. But `Refresh` also
fires on `ActiveUpdated`, that is **at every change of the document**, so with a single sheet open it was
enough to type in a cell for the bar to vanish under your hands.

The visibility of that bar already has an owner — the shell's `ApplyVisibility`, which ties it to the
opening of a document and to the *Tabs* setting — and two places deciding it are one place too many:
they contradict each other depending on who writes last. `Refresh` now **only rebuilds the tabs** and
does not touch visibility. So the bar is there as long as a document is open, even just one, and the
explicit switch to hide it remains.

**Verified live**: opened a single Ledger, typed in a cell and pressed Enter — the `Ledger1 ×` bar stays
in its place.

### Opening a document the ribbon starts from Home
Opening Ledger you found yourself on **Tools**. The strip keeps the chosen tab by comparing the
**title** — right while working, because selecting a shape or changing cell must not bring you back to
Home — but without a document the only existing tab is called *Tools* (Options and Theme), and when the
document opened that title still existed: a tab that had never been chosen was "restored".

The tab is now kept only **within the same module**: `RibbonModel` carries the module of the context it
is born from, and when it changes the strip starts again from the first tab. It also applies when moving
from Ledger to Folio, where the tabs are different.

**Verified live**: from the start page *Ledger* opens the sheet with **Home** active; choosing *Review*
and then clicking a cell the tab stays *Review*.

### The start page is a page, not an empty sheet with the ribbon on top
With the application open and no documents, **the ribbon** was visible — a *Tools* tab with *Options*
and *Theme*, the only two commands that exist without a document — and below, in the middle of a huge
white space, three cards with the module names. A toolbar towering over the welcome page says that you
are already inside a document that does not exist.

Now **ribbon and document tabs do not appear until a document is open**, and the place is taken by
`StartView`: title, the **Create** section with the three module cards (the accent line at the top, as
before, but a third of the space wide instead of a fixed 196 points), the **Recent documents** section
in two columns — type icon in the module color, name, folder with the tilde in place of home, date — and
*Open a document…* beside its label. At the bottom the palette shortcut, **derived from the gesture** and
not written in the text, so on Windows and Linux it will say Ctrl.

**The three cards did not look like buttons**, and it was true: white background on an almost white
background, no border, a shadow so faint it vanished and as the only hover signal a drop in opacity. Now
each has a **border**, the icon on a plate tinted with the accent at 12%, and above all it **says what it
does**: «＋ Nuovo documento» (+ New document) in the module color, with the extension beside it. On hover
the border takes the accent and the background a veil of the same color. A white box with a name inside
is not a button: it becomes one when it carries the verb.

The accent line at the top **went out of the rounded corners**: it is a rectangle three points tall as
long as the card, and at the ends it peeked past the curve of the border, which up close reads as a
crooked card. It is the same trap as the modal header and has the same solution: the card clips its
children, so the line follows the curve instead of crossing it.

The background is faint on purpose: a barely blue vertical veil and three halos in the module colors at
**4%**, cut by the bottom edge. It serves to make the screen look like a page and not an empty work area;
raising it would turn it into an advertisement.

The recent documents are not a separate list: the page **executes the commands** `shell.file.recent.N`
that the coordinator already registers, so what is seen here, in the *File* menu and in the palette is
the same thing. Vanished files do not appear, because `RecentDocuments` discards them on reading.

**A real defect found along this road**: closing the last document the start page **did not come back**.
`Close` set `Active` to null, but the shell kept showing the view of the closed document, with its ribbon
— the application stayed on a screen that no longer corresponded to anything. Now the shell follows
`DocumentClosed` and goes back home.

The screen was born as a view of its own and not as a method of the shell: `ShellWindow` had reached 435
lines and contained the construction of a module card.

**Verified live**: with five fake recent documents the page shows them in two columns with the right
icon per extension (.odt blue, .ods green, .odp red, .xlsx green), *Ledger* opens the sheet and ribbon
and tab make their appearance, and closing the tab goes back to the start page.
### All macro management lives in the IDE
*Tools ▸ Macros* had **three entries for the same thing**: "Macro…" opened the IDE on a scratch
sheet that did not know the document's macros, "Document macros…" was a form with four
fields — name, language, code in a multi-line box, and a *delete* checkbox — and "Organise
macros…" another form with the choice, the new name and two checkboxes to duplicate and delete.
Writing a macro meant pasting the code from one window to another, and the only place with
highlighting, completion and diagnostics was exactly the one that could not save.

Now the document's library is **a column of the IDE**: the list of macros on the left, *New*,
*Duplicate* and *Delete* below, the name and *Save* next to the language selector. Choosing a
macro opens it in the editor with **its own** language; renaming is changing the name and saving. The
language stops being a choice of the window and becomes what it had been in the model from the start:
a property of the macro.

No model was added: `IMacroLibrary` already existed in `PulseOffice.Document/Forms` with
`All`, `Find`, `Store`, `Remove` and its event. The editor just receives it — so Folio and Deck
will open the same IDE on their library without new code, and the macros hooked to the events
of form controls are the same ones written here.

Saving is **explicit**, and an empty name says so instead of inventing one: a macro without a
name cannot be called from a control, so silently saving it as "Macro1" would be an
object the user did not ask for. When switching macro, duplicating or deleting, whatever was being
written is still flushed into the library, otherwise a click in the list would throw away the
work.

In the command map, the reference suite's script-organiser command now points to the IDE, which is where that command really leads.

Removed in the same pass two lines that were read only once: the note on the engines above the
documentation — which said what the language selector already has written inside it, "JavaScript
(Jint) — default" — and the comment at the top of the example, which explained the same thing inside the
code. In place of the note there is the **Help** button, which is where it is needed: at the top of the column it
opens.

**Verified live**: with a document without macros the column says «Nessuna macro nel documento.
Con «Nuova» ne scrivi una» ("No macros in the document. Write one with «New»"); *New* proposes the name, `app.Log("ciao")` written in the editor and
*Save* makes "Macro" appear in the list; *Duplicate* creates "Macro 2" with the same code and *Run*
prints `ciao` in 264 ms; *Delete* removes it and going back to "Macro" the code is the one from before.

### Validation, filters and scenarios in the API (done)
Three more objects — `validation`, `filter`, `scenarios` — and the API reaches **one hundred and thirty members**
on nine objects. As always on top of what exists: the validation model with its three
alert levels (and only *Stop* really prevents writing), `ISheetFilter` and
`AutoFilterState` for filters, `IScenarioManager` for scenarios.

**The filter stays split in two as in the rest of the project**: the model says which rows do not
pass, the view hides them. The facade computes the set and hands it to
`IActiveSheetContext.ApplyRowFilter`, exactly as the filter menu does.

**The returned lists are .NET arrays**, and in JavaScript they behave well — index,
`.length`, `Array.from(...)` — but concatenating them directly into a string shows the name of the
type. It is a trace of the interop, not a defect of ours, and it is written in the documentation
pane instead of leaving the user to discover it.

**Verified live**: a macro writes six rows, puts a list validation on one column
and a numeric one on the other, captures the scenario "Base", writes an out-of-place value, turns on the
autofilter and filters on "Nord" — and the output says *validations 2, hidden 2*, that is the two
Sud rows really disappeared. The search "scenario" in the pane finds the six members with their
description.

### Pivot, printing and conditional formatting in the API (done)
Three new objects — `pivot`, `page`, `rules` — for a total of **one hundred and four members** and six
objects. Here too nothing new underneath: `IPivotCoordinator` for pivots (so subtotals
are computed from the data, not by summing the underlying totals), `ISheetPrintDocumentBuilder` and
`IPdfExporter` for printing, the sheet's rule model for conditional
formatting — which in fact **does not modify the cells**, it only changes their rendering.

**`print` could not be called `print`.** The JavaScript engine already defines a global
function `print` for output, and Python has its own: our object was shadowed and
`print.PrintArea(...)` answered "is not a function". It is called `page` (and `pagina`). A global
name is not an aesthetic choice: it collides or it does not.

**A defect found by counting**: the pivot turned out to be created **twice**, because
`PivotCoordinator.Apply` already registers the definition in the document and the facade added it
again. It was revealed by `pivot.Count` saying 2 after a single creation — that is, the API
querying itself.

**Verified live with a single macro**, and the strongest proof is the PDF that comes out of it: the macro
writes seven rows of data, adds **data bars** and a **value rule** (>55 in amber and
bold), creates the **pivot** Zone × Product, puts the page in **landscape** with
header "Riepilogo" and `&D`, and exports. The PDF read back with PDFKit measures **841×595** —
landscape — and contains the table, the pivot with Nord 160/30/190, Sud 60/50/110 and totals
220/80/300, the header with the date and the footer "1 / 1". The numbers are right: Nord Dado is
100 + 60.

### The macro editor has become an IDE (done)
The window was a text field with a button. Now it is an environment: **1180×760**, code editor
on the left, **searchable documentation** on the right, output and diagnostics below.

**Syntax highlighting and completion are real**, not an imitation: the editor is
`AvaloniaEdit`, which was already among the project's packages and had never been wired. The
completion is not a hand-written list: it asks **the active engine**
(`IScriptEngine.Complete`), which in turn queries the `ScriptApiCatalog` — that is, the rule
decided long ago, the scriptable API is **explicit metadata** and not reflection. It opens with the
dot, with the parenthesis and with Ctrl+Space.

**Nobody populated the API catalogue**: the structure existed and no content, so
completion was empty by definition. Now `SheetScriptApi` fills it, and each entry carries
signature, parameter types and a **translated** description with the usual rule of derived
keys (`api.sheet.<member>.summary`).

**Declaring an API means implementing it**: the catalogue listed things the facade did not
have, and it would have been a lie looking like documentation. `SheetScriptFacade` has
grown accordingly — `Range`, `WriteRange`, `Clear`, `Recalculate`, `Log`, `SheetCount`,
`UsedRange` — all on the UI thread and through the calculation engine, hence with
recalculation and undo.

**The documentation contains no code**, except where it is really needed, and then it is **JavaScript**:
the pane's header says that JavaScript is the **default** engine and that Python is a
first-class language with the same API and the same permissions — two different things that would
be easy to confuse. The language selector shows "JavaScript (Jint) — default",
and the aliases of the same API (`foglio` next to `sheet`) exist in the code but **are not
duplicated** in the list: an `IsAlias` keeps them out.

`IScriptOutput` was born because `Log` must end up in the output pane: the facade does not know
the window and the window does not know the facade, so the text passes through a service that
the editor captures for the duration of the run.

**The modal no longer closes with Escape.** While trying it I lost the code I had written: Escape closed
the whole window. In an editor that key serves to close the completion, not to throw away
the work.

Two things discovered while trying: without the `<StyleInclude>` of the AvaloniaEdit theme in `App.axaml`
the editor is **invisible** — it is there, it receives the text, it cannot be seen; and a `\n` written in a
translation file must be put as a real line break, otherwise the example appears on a single line with the
escape characters in plain view.

**Verified live in full**: highlighting (green comments, red strings, blue numbers),
completion after `sheet.` with the twelve members, the search "formula" finding `Write` with its
signature, double click inserting the symbol at the cursor, run in **JavaScript**
(writes 21, the formula gives 42, `Log` prints it, 304 ms) and the same thing in **Python** (7 × 6 = 42,
41 ms). Seven new tests on the tokenizer, which remains pure logic.

### Original Milestone 0
UI shell: `IWindowChrome` for the three systems, native macOS menu,
ribbon and menus fed by the command registry, modal service, settings schema.
Then the Ledger grid.

### Arrays: decision taken and implemented
Chose **(c) with (a) as the default**: dynamic arrays with spilling
(default) and classic array formulas confirmed over a range coexist
(needed to read existing ODF and XLSX). Implemented:

- `Spill` in the engine: range computed from the size of the result, all-or-nothing spilling,
  `#SPILL!` when the range is obstructed, release of the cells when the array
  shrinks, and **automatic retry** when the obstacle is removed (`_blockedSpills`).
- Reference `A1#` to the whole range, with a dependency on the anchor.
- `SetArrayFormula` for classic array formulas, with `#N/D` in the excess cells.
- **Propagation of operators over arrays**: `A1:A3>15` produces a vector of booleans,
  which is what makes `FILTRO(A1:A3; A1:A3>15)` writable.
- `FunctionImplementation` returns `EvalValue`, no longer `CellValue`: a function can
  produce an array. Scalar functions go through `FunctionBuilder` and do not notice.

### Lambdas: done
Implemented as **special forms** (`ISpecialForm`), not as functions: they receive the
arguments unevaluated, because LAMBDA must not touch its own body and LET must bind the
names before proceeding. The evaluator carries a nested `EvaluationScope` in which local
names hide those of the document, and `LambdaValue` captures the environment in which it was born:
it is a real closure, not a formula template.

The recursion limit **cannot live in the environment**: a recursive lambda always restarts
from the captured environment, so its depth stays constant while the recursion
grows. A separate call counter, per thread, is needed.

### The 9 missing functions, and why
They are not postponed by choice: **they query subsystems that do not exist yet**, and
writing them first would mean writing fictions.

| Function | Waiting for |
|---|---|
| `GETPIVOTDATA` | a working pivot table |
| `GOALSEEK`, `MULTIPLE.OPERATIONS` | the solver |
| `STYLE`, `COLOR` | the cell formatting layer |
| `WEBSERVICE`, `FILTERXML` | network access, with its permissions |
| `DDE` | data exchange between applications, Windows-specific |
| `MULTIRANGE` | the syntax of range unions in the parser |

### Deck: the declared ambition, and the first block that runs
**Deck must be as powerful as PowerPoint** and read/write **ODP and OOXML (PPTX) 100%** —
requested by the user. "100%" here means the same as for Ledger: either a feature crosses **both**
formats, or the loss is declared in a `CheckFidelity` with its own code. The list to
cover is the union of what the reference suite and PowerPoint can do: masters and themes, layouts, transitions
per slide, **animations** (entrance, emphasis, exit, motion paths) with their
timeline and their triggers, **sounds**, **events/interactions** (on-click actions, links,
macros), media, speaker notes, presentation sponsorship.

So as not to stiffen the architecture, **the model is born already able to carry all this as
data**, even before playback exists: `Slide.Transition` (`SlideTransition`),
`Slide.Animations` (`AnimationEffect`: category, trigger, delay, duration, repetitions, path,
sound) and `Slide.Interactions` (`InteractiveAction`: on click → slide, link, macro,
sound). Retrofitting them later would have touched every serializer, which is exactly the defect to
avoid.

Development proceeds **in verifiable blocks** (the user's choice). Order: 1) model + rendering +
text editing *(this block, done)*; 2) masters, themes and layouts; 3) ODP and OOXML formats with
round-trip on real files from the reference suite and PowerPoint and `CheckFidelity`; 4) transitions and animations
(data → editor → playback); 5) presentation mode, speaker notes, presenter
screen; 6) media, sounds, events and interactions.

**Done in this first block** — and tried live:
- The core `PulseOffice.Presentations` (without Avalonia): `Presentation` (slide list,
  16:9 or 4:3 size), `Slide` (background, notes, transition, animations, interactions, elements),
  `SlideElement` (text or `EmbeddedObject`, so **charts, shapes, images, data tables and formulas
  from Ledger live in Deck without new code**, as planned by cross-app objects), `SlideText`
  (paragraphs with body, bold, alignment, bulleted list), and the five base layouts.
- The **factory is an injectable service** (`ISlideFactory`), not a class of static methods:
  it creates the layouts with their placeholders, **clones** (Prototype, with re-id of elements and
  animations) and **re-lays out** keeping the text of filled placeholders. Structural actions
  (`DeckActions`) are **undoable** commands on top of the `UndoStack` (Command pattern via
  `DelegateAction`): new, duplicate, delete, move, change layout, edit text.
- Rendering is an `ISlideRenderer` (strategy) reused by the large canvas and the thumbnails, which
  **delegates embedded objects to `IDrawingObjectRenderer`** — the same drawer as Ledger.
  `SlideView` is the control that lays out the slide letterboxed and does hit-testing; `DeckView`
  composes the slide list on the left, the canvas in the centre and **inline text editing**
  (double click on a placeholder → overlaid box; Enter confirms a title, Shift/⌘+Enter a
  body, Esc cancels, a click outside confirms).
- Hooked to the shell like Ledger: `IDeckDocumentFactory` creates an `OpenDocument` of the
  Presentations module, and *File ▸ New Deck document* opens a real presentation with its tab,
  the red accent and "ODP" in the status bar.

**Verified live**: new presentation with the title slide; *New* adds a
"Title and content" slide; double click on the title, "Relazione trimestrale" typed and
confirmed with Enter appears bold and centred both on the canvas and in the thumbnail; ⌘Z
brings it back empty and removes the modified dot. Six tests on the core (factory, clone, re-layout,
carrying transition and animations, moving, paragraph cutting), all green.

**Not yet done, and declared**: media, sounds and events/interactions.

### Deck: all layouts and all animation presets (done)
Rule set by the user: Deck must cover **all the layouts and all the animations** of the reference suite
and of Microsoft Office. Two subsystems, same idea: carry the **native identifier** in the
model and keep its table in **one place only**, shared between the two mappers, so a value that
the editor does not know still survives the round trip and the two tables cannot diverge.

**Animation presets** (`AnimationPresetRegistry`): a preset has three faces — canonical name,
OOXML identifier, ODF identifier of the reference suite — kept in a single piece of data that both mappers
read. Fifty known presets across entrance, emphasis, exit and path. An **unknown** preset
is not lost: OOXML keeps it as `ooxml-<id>`, ODF verbatim. The two fidelity tests
that declared animations and transitions as losses had become false (they are now serialized) and
were moved onto interactive actions, which really remain unwritten.

**Layouts: eleven, the complete set of PowerPoint and the reference suite** (`SlideLayout` + `SlideLayoutRegistry`):
title slide, title and content, section header, two content, **comparison**,
**title only**, blank, **content with caption**, **picture with caption**, **vertical
text**, **vertical title and text**. Before there were five, and the readers **guessed** the
layout from the geometry of the placeholders — so even the section header did not survive.
Now the layout carries its **native type**: in OOXML each layout is a `slideLayout` with its own
`Type` (`title`, `obj`, `secHead`, `twoObj`, `twoTxTwoObj`, `titleOnly`, `blank`, `objTx`, `picTx`,
`vertTx`, `vertTitleAndTx`), one part per type used, and the slide refers to it; in ODF it is the name
`presentation:presentation-page-layout-name` (`AL-*`). Reading prefers the declared type and
falls back on inference only if it is missing. `MasterFactory` now has a template for each one, with the placeholders
in the right place (captions, picture, vertical text), and the inspector's selector is generated
**from the enum** — adding a layout adds its entry without touching the view.

**Verified with the real reference suite, in both directions and for all eleven layouts.** A deck with every
layout, written by us in PPTX and converted by the reference suite into ODP, comes back with the eleven `AL-*`
intact; written in ODP and converted into PPTX, it comes back with the eleven OOXML `type` intact — data
really read from the attribute, not inferred. Twenty-two round-trip tests (eleven per format) plus the
nine of the preset registry.

### Deck: formula, chart and table on the slide (rendering done)
The last three insertions that were missing. The knot was not inserting them — they are `EmbeddedObject` — but
**drawing them**: the `DrawingObjectRenderer` does not know them (it renders only shapes, images, vectors).
The rendering already existed elsewhere, decoupled from sheets, and was composed:
- **Formula**: `FormulaObject` (linear expression) → `IFormulaParser.Parse` → `IFormulaRenderer.Render`
  on `DrawingContext`. No tie to sheets. Command *Formula*, with a small form asking for
  the expression. **Verified live**: `sqrt {a^2 + b^2}` appears typeset properly, radical
  and superscripts.
- **Chart**: `ChartRenderer.Render(context, definition, ChartData, bounds)` consumes **inline data**,
  not a sheet — extraction from the sheet (`ChartDataExtractor`) is the only coupled piece and is not
  needed here. Added `ChartDefinition.InlineData` (optional) to carry the data onto the slide;
  the *Chart* command inserts a column chart with sample data. **Verified**: columns, axes,
  legend and title appear on the slide's sheet.
- **Table**: `DataTableObject` with an **inline** `Snapshot` (columns + rows, no query);
  `IDataTableRenderer.Render` draws from the snapshot, without a database. The *Table* command inserts
  a 3×3 grid. **Verified**: header, banded rows and grid lines.

`SlideRenderer` gains three branches (`FormulaObject`/`ChartDefinition`/`DataTableObject`) with the three
renderers as fields (stateless), and the references to `PulseOffice.Formulas` and `PulseOffice.Data.UI`.
All three are selected and deleted like the other objects.

**Declared**: formula, chart and table **do not yet cross the two formats** (they remain in the
loss `PPTX004`/`ODP004`): their native serialization (chart part, table, MathML/OMML) is
a job of its own. They render and present in-app; saving loses them, declared.

Measured coverage of the reference suite's presentation commands: from **31 to 34 of 387 (8.8 %)**.

### Deck: review of enablement, tab by tab
A pass over all of Deck's ribbon tabs to check that grey tells the truth.
The verdict is almost all fine, and consistent with "Off, not gone": **Design** turns off the
**active** layout and theme and turns on the others; **Transitions** turns off the current transition;
**View** turns off the active view mode; **Insert** is always on with a deck open;
**Slide Show** turns everything on except "Present a custom one" until one exists;
**Home** turns on the formatting objects only with a placeholder/object selected.

A real defect found this way: **"Add animation" was on even on a
slide with nothing to animate** (a Blank layout, or after removing the placeholders), and clicking it
did nothing — the dead click that this project considers worse than a missing command. Now
it is enabled only if there is an element to animate and **animates the selected object** if there is one, otherwise the
first text, otherwise the first element. **Verified live**: on a Blank layout the command is
grey; with text or an object selected it becomes active again.

### Deck: the ribbon opened all grey, and the thumbnails had too many buttons
Two defects reported by looking at a freshly opened Deck. The first was real and big: **almost all
ribbon and menu commands were off**, and they stayed off. The second, a matter of form: the thumbnail
strip had at its bottom four buttons (*New*, *Duplicate*, *Delete*, *Media*) that repeat
commands already in the ribbon.

**Why everything was grey.** The ribbon re-evaluates enablement only when the **shell
context** changes (`workspace.ContextChanged`). Ledger updates that context from the view at every selection
change (`LedgerView` calls `workspace.UpdateContext`); **Deck did not**. The `DeckView`
announces itself (`IActiveDeckContext.Attach`) *after* the ribbon has already been built — with `Target`
still null, hence every Deck command off — and nobody told the ribbon to rebuild. Now
startup binds `IActiveDeckContext.Changed` to `ShellWindow.RefreshSurfaces`: when the Deck context
attaches or the selection changes, ribbon and menus are rebuilt and re-read the updated state. `DeckView.Select`
re-announces the context, so changing slide too updates "Move up/down" and "Delete". The
grey that remains is the right one: *Delete* with a single slide, the font until a placeholder
is selected.

**The thumbnails lose the buttons and get a context menu.** The four buttons at the bottom of the
strip are gone; right-clicking a thumbnail now opens a menu **projected from the registry**
(`IContextMenuFactory.Build("slide")`), like Ledger's sheet tabs: the
`deck.slide.*` commands declare a `ContextPaths` (*Manage*: new, duplicate, delete, hide; *Order*:
move up/down) and appear there without dedicated code, already translated and context-sensitive. A
trap solved along the way: opening the menu after `Select` failed because `Select→Sync` **rebuilds
the strip** and detaches the thumbnail under the menu — now the menu opens on the `DeckView`, which is stable.

**Verified live**: opening a new Deck, *New slide*, *Duplicate* and *Hide* are
active (before, all grey); clicking the «Titolo» ("Title") placeholder the Font group lights up; the
right click on a thumbnail opens «GESTISCI: Nuova / Duplica / Nascondi» ("MANAGE: New / Duplicate / Hide"). The strip no longer has the
buttons at the bottom.

### Deck D6: sections (done)
Sections group slides, as in PowerPoint. **A section is marked on the
slide that starts it** (`Slide.SectionName`): the section goes from that slide up to the
next marked one. It is PowerPoint's form and converts without translation.

`SlideSections` is **pure, tested logic** in `PulseOffice.Presentations`: it groups the
slides under the start marker, and finds the section of a slide by walking
backwards to the first marker. Duplicating a slide does **not** copy the
marker, otherwise a duplicate would become the start of a second section with the same name.

**Surface**: the `deck.section.*` commands (add, rename, remove) live in the thumbnail's **context
menu** — projected from the registry like everything else — under the
*Section* group, and in the palette; not in the ribbon, which remains a curated subset. Enablement is
sensitive: *Add* only if the slide is not already a section start, *Rename* and *Remove*
only if it belongs to a section. The filmstrip draws a header before each slide
that starts a section; double-clicking the header renames it inline, and *Rename section*
from the menu opens a field prefilled with the current name. All undoable.

**Only one format knows them, and it is declared.** OOXML writes them in the presentation's extension
list (`p14:sectionLst` with `p14:section`/`p14:sldIdLst`, slides cited by
numeric identifier); the element is built as `p:extLst` with the p14 content in
`InnerXml`, and on reading the presentation's `OuterXml` is parsed — robust and independent
of the SDK version. **The reference suite has no sections**, so in ODF they are a declared loss
(`ODP011`), not a silence.

**Verified live and with the reference suite**: on three slides, *Add section* from the menu of the
second makes the header «SEZIONE 1» ("SECTION 1") appear; *Rename section* opens the prefilled field and
takes it to «INTRODUZIONE»; and a PPTX with two sections written→read back comes back with «Intro» and «Corpo» in
their places, and opens in the reference suite without errors. Sections are not a menu entry of the reference suite
(they are PowerPoint's), so the measured coverage stays **43 of 387**: it is a feature **beyond**
the reference suite, towards parity with PowerPoint.

Tools note: `uiprobe/click` now has `--double`, which sets the `mouseEventClickState` for a
real double click — two separate invocations are too slow for Avalonia to connect them. Even
so the synthetic double click does not always arrive as `DoubleTapped`, which is why
rename has **also** the command in the menu, which is verifiable and more discoverable.

### Deck D7: export to PDF, images, HTML and video (done)
Deck now exports to **PDF** (slides one per page, **notes**, n-up **handouts**:
2/3/4/6/9), to **images** (one PNG per slide), to **HTML** (one page with the slides
embedded) and to **mp4 video**. It rests on `IPageCanvas`/`PulseOffice.Formats.Pdf` as planned by the
plan.

**H.264 video is provided by the operating system, one encoder per OS behind `IVideoEncoder`** — the same
discipline as `IPrintService`/`ISecretVault`/`IScannerService` (rule 15, no `#if`): an
`IVideoEncoderProvider` chooses at runtime from `RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform`. An mp4/H.264 encoder
in **pure C# does not exist** without native binaries; every route is a native codec, either the OS's or shipped. Choice:
the **OS's** codec, which installs nothing on Windows and macOS.

- **macOS → VideoToolbox**: `VTCompressionSession` is a **C** API, hence direct P/Invoke to
  `VideoToolbox.framework` (the CFString constants of the properties are read with `dlsym`); it produces the
  H.264 stream and **we write the mp4 container ourselves** (`Mp4Writer`, the ISO-BMFF boxes, like PDF/ODF).
- **Windows → Media Foundation** via **Vortice.MediaFoundation** (managed wrapper, MIT, no binary
  shipped): the *Sink Writer* encodes H.264 into mp4.
- **Linux → ffmpeg** if present; otherwise the command **says to install it** (like the scanner).

Each slide is a frame, duration from the `AfterTime` transition time or 3 s by default.
Declared: the frames capture the **final state** of the slide (internal animations are not
rendered in the video).

**The muxer's lesson, found by the real reader.** The first mp4 had structurally correct boxes
but AVFoundation rejected it (*Failed to load asset*): `mvhd` and `mdhd` lacked the two
*creation/modification time* fields, and all following fields shifted by four bytes. It is the same
lesson as ODF/PDF ("re-reading only what we write is not enough"): with the corrected fields,
`avmediainfo` reads the file as **H.264, right dimensions, decoding supported, 0 errors**.

**Verified live on macOS, end-to-end**: from a three-slide Deck, *Export as video* →
native panel → `deckvideo.mp4`, which **AVFoundation** reads as H.264 1600×900, 9 s (3×3 s),
decodable, "Movie analyzed with 0 error". **Windows (Media Foundation) is written and wired but
not verified** on this machine (it is a Mac): it must be tried on a real Windows. Linux via ffmpeg as
above.

**The real infrastructure piece: the image in the PDF.** The PDF could not draw images — the
sheets and shapes have always been paths and text. Now `IPageCanvas.DrawImage` exists, the
`PdfContentCanvas` emits an image XObject (`q  w 0 0 h x y cm  /ImgN Do  Q`), and `PdfExporter`
writes the image object (`/Subtype /Image /ColorSpace /DeviceRGB /BitsPerComponent 8`, RGB
samples with `FlateDecode`) and cites it in the page's `/XObject` resources. It is **reusable**
infrastructure: from here Ledger too will be able to put a real raster image in a PDF. `AvaloniaPageCanvas`
draws it on screen for the preview.

**Slides become pixels** with `ISlideImageRenderer`: a `RenderTargetBitmap` drawn by the
**same** `SlideRenderer` as the editor (no second rendering), with the export palette
(transparent placeholder and border, so the «Titolo» hints do not appear). It exposes the PNG and the
raw RGB pixels for the PDF. `DeckPrintable` (an `IPrintableDocument`) lays out the rasters: one
slide per page full-sheet, the n-up grid with bordered cells, or the
slide above and the notes below. The commands (`deck.export.pdf/images/html`, tab *Slide Show ▸
Export*, menu *File ▸ Export*) rasterize, build the document and write; the HTML embeds
the PNGs in base64. Icons and five languages, clean startup audit.

**Verified live in full**: from a four-slide Deck, *Export to PDF* opens the
window with the layout (slides, notes, handouts 2/3/4/6/9 translated), the native save
panel writes the file, and the PDF produced — read back with **PDFKit** — is a handout of
**two pages** with **four XObject images**, A4 format, `DeviceRGB`, bordered cells. Unit
test on the image XObject in `PdfExporter` (green). Coverage of the reference suite's presentation commands: **47 of 387 (12.1%)**.

With this **D7 is closed**; D8 remains (finishing touches: fields, headers/footers, grid/guides, options).

### Document versions and digital signatures for all modules (done)
**Versions**: `DocumentVersion`/`DocumentVersionCollection` moved from `PulseOffice.Sheets` to
`PulseOffice.Document.Versions` — they were generic but lived in the sheets module. `Presentation`
now has its versions, ODP writes and reads them back in the same `Versions/` folder used by the reference suite
(`OdfVersionMapper` reused, with the MIME type as a parameter), and PPTX **declares** them lost
(`PPTX014`, like `XLSX022`: OOXML has no versions in the file). The command belongs to the shell
(`ShellDocumentCommands`); the Strategy exposes the collection, and the snapshot is taken with `WriteTo` in the
module's native format.

Two defects of Ledger's implementation, corrected while moving it:
- **saving or deleting a version did not mark the document as modified**: it wrote into the
  collection without going through the history, so closing without saving the version was lost
  without any question. Now they are history actions, undoable; undoing a deletion
  puts the version back **in its place** (`Restore`), not at the end;
- `OdfVersionMapper.Write` was a **lazy iterator with side effects**: it wrote into the package
  only if the caller enumerated the result. Now it is a normal method.

**Signatures**: `ShellSignatureCommands` (document signatures, signing an existing PDF). The
signing service already worked on any ODF file, `.odp` included; the tie with Ledger was the **global**
tracker fed only by opening sheets — in Deck it would not have known which file to sign.
The command now uses the path of the active document, and updates the tracker only to keep
Ledger's indicator right. Macro signing and the signature line remain Ledger's. Signatures
remain in the ribbon in Ledger (*Review*) with a per-module rule.

**Verified**: an ODP with versions opens in the reference suite, and a test checks that **every entry
of the ZIP is declared in the manifest** (the rule that, when violated, gets the file rejected); an `.odp`
is signed with a certificate generated by the test — not with the user's keychain, which would have
asked for access. Live in Deck: saving a version marks "Deck1 •", ⌘Z removes it and the
document goes back to unmodified. A known limit remains: saving a signed document rewrites the
package and **loses the signatures** without warning; the reference suite warns. See the Open points.

### Remote stores, sharing and edit mode for all modules — and Deck respects read-only (done)
`ShellRemoteCommands` replaces `LedgerRemoteCommands`: open and save to a remote store, check
out, cancel, check in. They were already almost generic; the two module-specific pieces were opening
(now the generic document router) and saving (now the `IDocumentSaver`s that both
modules already implement for the modification guard). Sharing and *Edit mode* moved
to `ShellDocumentCommands`; sharing stays in the ribbon in Ledger (*Review*) with a per-module
rule, and in Deck it is in the menu.

**Deck did not respect read-only at all.** Bringing *Edit mode* to it, the document became
"read-only" and stayed entirely editable: no Deck command declared the
forbidden state. It would have been a switch that moves nothing. Two levels, as for Ledger:
- **a safety net at the single point** every modification goes through: `DeckActions.Do` refuses
  when the document is read-only (a `Func<bool>` on the `OpenDocument`, which is born after the
  actions). Verified that **all** the public methods of `DeckActions` go through there. The
  inline text editor does not open either;
- **the commands turn off**: every Deck command that modifies now declares `ReadOnly` among the forbidden
  states. The helpers that also served harmless commands have an explicit `edits` parameter —
  "Play animation", "Copy", "Select all", slide show, export,
  navigation and views stay on. The properties panel and the Theme/Layout drop-downs are disabled following the
  document.

**A false coverage, corrected**: in the spreadsheet command map, the reference suite's "open in design mode" command (for
forms) was mapped onto `ledger.file.openReadOnly`, that is "Open read-only" — a different feature,
and **with no effect** (a flag nobody read). The bogus entry was removed and the spreadsheet row
marked **missing**: coverage honestly drops to 412/413. Design mode on opening is a document flag
in the reference suite; it will really be done in the forms block, where the presentation module asks for it too.

**Verified live in Deck**: *Edit mode* turns off New/Duplicate/Hide slide, the
formatting and the panel, leaves Play on, and removing it brings everything back; the remote
store navigator opens from Deck.

### Sending by mail, Bluetooth and browser preview for all modules (done)
`ShellSendCommands` replaces `LedgerMailCommands` and Ledger's web preview: e-mail,
by mail as **OpenDocument**, as **Microsoft Office** (xlsx or pptx depending on the module), as
PDF, via Bluetooth, and preview in the browser. The Strategy has grown by what is needed —
native and Office extension, `WriteTo` (the module writes its own document in the requested format) and
`RenderHtml` (Ledger with the sheet's HTML writer, Deck with `IDeckPublisher`). *More
online dictionaries* too, which only opens an address, has moved to the shell.

**"E-mail…" did not attach the document**: it composed a message with only the subject. In
the reference suite that entry sends the document, and it is what the word promises. Now it attaches the document
in the format in which it is saved (in ODF if it is not yet saved), and if the mail program cannot
carry attachments it says so instead of composing an empty message. Attachments are born in their own
temporary folder, so the file carries the document's name without collisions.

The spreadsheet entries that named the sheet format ("as OpenDocument spreadsheet", "as Microsoft
Excel") are now generic ("as OpenDocument", "as Microsoft Office"): one command for two
modules.

The real sending was not tried live: it would open the user's mail client, the Bluetooth transfer or the
browser without them having asked. Tried that the entries exist and are enabled in Deck
and in Ledger; the pieces they rest on — the format writers and Deck's HTML — are already tested.

### Document properties for all modules, and custom fields in OOXML (done)
*File ▸ Document properties…* is now a shell command (`ShellDocumentCommands`) that asks
the module for the properties through the Strategy (`IDocumentOperations.Properties`). For Deck the
model was needed: **`Presentation.Properties`** did not exist, ODP wrote a fixed `meta.xml` with only
the generator and PPTX no `docProps`. Deck's save now updates modification date and
counter (`MarkSaved`) like Ledger's.

**One mapper per format family, not per module**: `OdfMetaMapper` (extracted from
`OdsWriter`/`OdsReader`) serves ODS and ODP, `OoxmlCorePropertiesMapper` (extracted from
`XlsxWriter`/`XlsxReader`) serves XLSX and PPTX; the private copies were removed. ODS keeps its
fallback values for title, author and creation date.

Three defects found along the way:
- **Changing the properties did not mark the document as modified**: the command wrote
  into the object without going through the history, so closing without saving the work was lost
  without any question. Now the change is a history action: it marks the document, is undone
  with ⌘Z, and undoing back to the saved state the document returns to unmodified.
- **XLSX silently lost the custom fields** of the properties — no declaration in
  `CheckFidelity`, that is the violation of rule 7 that this project considers the worst. OOXML
  can describe them (`docProps/custom.xml`, `CustomFilePropertiesPart` with `vt:lpwstr`): now they are
  written and read back, in XLSX and in PPTX.
- The form used Italian keys (`titolo`, `argomento`…): now English, as the canonical form requires.

**Verified with the real reference suite, in both directions**: from our PPTX the reference suite carries into `meta.xml`
title, keyword and the custom field «Reparto»; from our ODP it carries them into
`docProps/core.xml` and `docProps/custom.xml`. **Live in Deck**: the properties open, the written title
marks "Deck1 •", ⌘Z removes it and brings the document back to unmodified.

### Printing for all modules: one Strategy per module, and the ribbon per module (done)
First piece of the "file operations" block: print, preview and printer settings
existed only in Ledger. Now they are shell commands (`ShellPrintCommands`) that ask the
**module of the active document** for what is its own, through a Strategy:

- **`IDocumentOperations`** (in `PulseOffice.Shell`): suggested name and printable document. The
  implementations live in the modules — `LedgerDocumentOperations` delegates to the sheet's print
  builder, `DeckDocumentOperations` to **`IDeckPublisher`**, extracted from `DeckExportCommands`
  (suggested name, printable, HTML, renderer): export and printing now use the same
  construction instead of two. `IDocumentOperationsCatalog` chooses per module. It will grow with the
  other operations (properties, versions, mail, templates) instead of multiplying
  `if (Module == …)` in the commands.
- **The ribbon can place a shell command differently per module.** Print and preview
  are in *Layout ▸ Page* in Ledger and at the head of *Slide Show ▸ Export* in Deck: with a
  single position per id, Deck would have had a "Layout" tab with only two entries. The map's
  rules now accept the form **`id@Module`** (`CommandLayout.ModulePathsFor`,
  `CommandDefinition.RibbonPaths`/`RibbonPathIn`), and the **rank used to order the tabs is
  that of the current module's rule**: the first version took the qualified rule highest
  in the map — Deck's — and in Ledger the Layout tab rose before Home. Seen
  on screen, corrected, and guarded by a test.
- **Printer settings did nothing**: it stored printer, copies and duplex in properties
  nobody read, and the *duplex* checkbox did not even reach the print request
  (`PrintRequest` lacked the field). Now the choices are `IPrintPreferences`, the print
  window starts from that printer and those copies, and duplex is **declared**:
  `IPrintService.SupportsDuplex` — CUPS does it with `-o sides=two-sided-long-edge`, the Windows print
  verb does not, and there the checkbox does not appear.
- **Two conflicting shortcuts, found by a new check.** Startup now reports the commands
  **active together** that share a shortcut (`CommandRegistry.ConflictingShortcuts`:
  same module, or shell versus module; pure, tested logic). It found two in the whole
  application: Ledger's print preview used **⇧⌘P, the palette's shortcut** —
  and since between two equal gestures the module's wins, in Ledger ⇧⌘P opened the preview while
  the titlebar advertises the palette — and *edit comment* shared ⌃⌥M with the macro
  editor. Now the preview is **⇧⌘O** and the comment **⌃⌥C**, the reference suite's shortcuts.

**Verified live**: in Ledger ⇧⌘P opens the palette and *Layout ▸ Page* still has Print and
Preview, with the tabs in the usual order; in Deck *Slide Show ▸ Export* starts with
Print and Preview, the preview shows the slide (empty placeholders, on purpose, are not
printed), the print window lists the system printer, and after *Printer
settings* with 2 copies printing starts from 2. Nothing was sent to the real printer.

Known limit, pre-existing and now written down: on Windows printing goes through the shell verb, which
**ignores printer, copies and page range** that the window asks for anyway. It must be made
honest like duplex (declaring what the service can do) or replaced with real
printing; see the Open points.

### Deck: navigation between slides and slide name (done)
Six navigation commands — first, previous, next, last, *go to slide…* and
**last modified slide** — in *Slide ▸ Go to*, and **renaming** the slide.
None of the seven goes in the ribbon: PowerPoint does not put them there, one navigates from the filmstrip.

**The ribbon is now an explicit choice for Deck too.** The prefix rules `deck.slide.`,
`deck.insert.` and `deck.view.` put **any** new command of those families in the ribbon:
with the two hundred entries still missing, navigation and special characters would have ended up in the ribbon by
chance. Converted into exact rules for the commands that were there, in the same order: today's
interface does not change, and what goes into the ribbon from now on is decided by a line written on purpose. It is the
same correction already made for `deck.format.`.

**The slide's name is the identifier in ODF**, and this decides everything. `draw:name` is the
name the reference suite shows in the navigator, but it is also what custom presentations cite
(`presentation:pages`), the start slide (`presentation:start-page`) and "go to
slide" links (`#name`). So the written name must be the same in all those places:
`SlideNames.PageName` (chosen name, otherwise the id) is the only source, and the writer translates ids
into names wherever it cites them. On reading back, the id is `draw:name` (references stay consistent) and the chosen
name is that same value **unless it is automatic** (`slideN`, `pageN`): the reference suite calls
slides without a name `page1`. In OOXML the name is in `p:cSld/@name`, separate from the ids.
`SlideNames` is pure, tested logic: an empty name goes back to the automatic name, and two slides
cannot have the same **effective** name — not even a chosen name equal to the id of
another, unrenamed one, because in ODF they would become two pages with the same name.

**A pre-existing defect found while trying**: `GoToSlide` changed slide **without
re-announcing the context**, so ribbon and menus stayed in the state of the previous slide —
after "First slide", "Move up" stayed on. *Find next* uses it too. Now it goes
through `Select`, the only route that closes the editor, changes slide and re-announces. And
the "last modified" after *New slide* pointed to the previous slide, because
`Changed` fires before focus passes to the new one: the slide that
an action brings into focus counts too.

**Verified with the real reference suite, in both formats**: from our ODP the reference suite keeps
«Conclusioni»; from our PPTX it reads `cSld/@name` and writes `draw:name="Conclusioni"`, calling
the unnamed one `page1`. Round-trip test in ODP with a custom presentation, a
"go to" link and the start slide pointing to the renamed slide: after the
round trip they still resolve. **Verified live**: enablement states follow the
current slide, "last modified" goes back to the third, rename is prefilled on
reopening, and the duplicate is rejected with a message in the status bar.

### The shell inside Ledger: application commands moved where they belong
Starting the missing entries of the reference suite's presentation menus, the first discovery was that many existed
**already, but inside Ledger**: `LedgerShellExtraCommands` was literally the shell written in the
sheets module — side panel, toolbars, customise, interface, XML filters — with
`Module = Sheets` and enabled only with an active sheet. In Deck they did not exist at all.
Rule 2-bis and rule 10: they are moved, not duplicated.

- **`ShellInterfaceCommands`** (next to `ShellCommands`, without a module): `shell.view.statusBar`,
  `shell.view.sidebar`, `shell.view.toolbars`, `shell.tools.customize`,
  `shell.tools.userInterface`, `shell.tools.xmlFilters`, plus two commands that did not exist:
  **`shell.file.close`** (⌘W) and **`shell.file.quit`**. Close and Quit go through the **same
  modification guard** as the tab ✕ and window closing:
  `IShellPresenter` now has `CloseActiveDocumentAsync` and `RequestQuit`, and `ShellWindow`
  implements them reusing what was there. Before, in the spreadsheet map, "Close" and "Quit" were marked done only
  as a note (the ✕), without a command.
- **A real defect**: `ledger.view.statusBar` **did not touch the status bar** but hid the
  **sheet tabs** (`_sheetTabs.IsVisible`). In the past the title had been corrected, not the
  behaviour. Now the status bar is the shell command, which toggles the setting
  `interface.statusBarVisible` already followed by `ApplyVisibility`; the old command becomes what
  it does: `ledger.view.sheetTabs`, «Schede dei fogli» ("Sheet tabs"), with its icon. `IShellViewOptions`
  carries `SheetTabsVisible`.
- Ledger keeps only what is its own: `LedgerPanelCommands` (styles in the panel, development
  tools, which inspect the active sheet).
- The two coverage maps follow the ids: **the spreadsheet map stays 413/413**; the presentation map gains status
  bar, panel, toolbars, customise, XML filters, close, quit.

**Verified live, in both modules**: in Deck the View tab now has the group
*Show* (status bar, toolbars, side panel); "Status bar" really hides it and puts it
back; in Ledger "Sheet tabs" hides the «Foglio1» tab leaving the status bar in
its place; File ▸ Close closes an unmodified document without questions and, with a change,
shows «Deck1 ha modifiche non salvate» ("Deck1 has unsaved changes"); Quit goes through the same question, and with «Non salvare» ("Don't save")
the application exits cleanly, with no crash reports or recovery copies left behind.

**Found along the way, corrected separately**: the key `autocorrect.explanation` was **duplicated** in
all five languages with two different texts. The parser keeps the last one, so Ledger's
replacement list showed the explanation of the options window. The keys were separated, and
a test (`NessunaChiaveECompareDueVolte`) reads the **raw** JSON of each language — a normal
parser merges duplicates and would not see them; verified that it fails on the previous file.

New tool: `tools/uiprobe/windowshot` captures **only** the application window, never the
whole screen, which would contain the windows of the user's other applications.

### Deck: text style of master placeholders in both formats (done)
The `Seed` of each layout placeholder (a `TextParagraph`: size, bold, italic,
alignment, colour/role, major/minor font, bulleted list) **was not written in any
format**, and worse: the two readers **silently discarded it** and regenerated it from the standard
per role — a loss that was not even declared. Now it crosses both formats.

- **OOXML**: in the layout placeholder's `p:txBody`, `a:lstStyle/a:lvl1pPr` with `algn`,
  `a:buChar`/`a:buNone` and `a:defRPr` (`sz`, `b`, `i`, colour as `a:schemeClr` — so the colour
  **role** survives — and font as **`+mj-lt`/`+mn-lt`**, the native reference to the
  theme font). The reader converts it back into the seed.
- **ODF**: one `style:style family="presentation"` per (layout, role) in `office:styles`
  (`sd_<layout>_<role>`), with `fo:font-size`/`font-weight`/`font-style`/`font-family`/`color` and
  `fo:text-align`; the bulleted list as `style:list-style-name` towards a shared
  `text:list-style`. The reader finds them by name.
- **The trap, found by the tests**: in the «Chiaro» ("Light") theme the major and minor fonts are **the same**
  (Inter), so distinguishing major/minor by name is impossible. OOXML solves it with the
  native references `+mj-lt`/`+mn-lt`. In ODF the theme does not exist (`ODP010`, now explicit on
  fonts too): the reader infers major/minor from the name **only if the two fonts differ**,
  otherwise it keeps the standard value. Colour in ODF comes back absolute, as already declared.
- `MasterEditing.WithPlaceholderSeed` (same shape as `WithPlaceholderBounds`). Test
  `MasterPlaceholderTextStyleSurvives` in both suites with a seed **different from the standard** (so
  the old silent discard would have been seen): Odf 173, OpenXml 167 green.

**Verification with the reference suite, honest**: the files in both formats open and convert to PDF, and the
PPTX contains exactly the expected `lstStyle`. But **it is not proven that the reference suite applies the
per-layout style**: it uses a per-master model and, converting our PPTX into ODP, it does not
carry over the italic or alignment of the modified seed. It is PowerPoint's behaviour that the
schema describes; I do not declare it interoperable with the reference suite until I see it.

### Deck: native grayscale and image crop in both formats (done)
Of the image filters (`ImageFilter`: grayscale, sepia, invert, mosaic) and the **crop**, what
has a native equivalent in **both** formats now crosses the formats; the rest remains a
declared loss, honestly narrowed.

- **Grayscale**: OOXML `a:grayscl` inside `a:blip`; ODF `draw:color-mode="greyscale"` in the
  `style:graphic-properties` of the frame's graphic style. Full round trip.
- **Crop**: OOXML `a:srcRect` (l/t/r/b in thousandths of a percent); ODF `fo:clip="rect(T R B L)"`
  in the graphic style (sets of lengths computed from the fractions × the frame's bounds). The
  reader converts back to fractions. Our own round trip exact.
- **Sepia, invert, mosaic**: no **symmetric** equivalent in the two formats (ODF has no
  sepia/invert/mosaic; emitting them only in OOXML would violate rule 7) — they remain rendered on
  screen and declared `ODP015`/`PPTX010`, now narrowed to these three.
- **Verified with the real reference suite**: a grayscale+crop image in ODP and PPTX opens and converts to
  PDF; and converting our **PPTX→ODP the reference suite re-emits `color-mode="greyscale"` *and*
  `fo:clip`** — it really interpreted both the grayscale (`a:grayscl`) and the crop (`a:srcRect`),
  it did not ignore them. (Its clip values differ from ours because it measures the clip
  on the image's natural size, not on the frame: the crop is honoured, not byte-identical
  — expected.) Test `ImageGrayscaleAndCropSurvive` in both suites.

### Deck: native slide background image in both formats (done)
The background image (`Slide.BackgroundImage`, a `RasterImageObject`) was rendered on screen but
declared as loss `ODP016`/`PPTX011`. Now it crosses **both** formats.

- **ODF**: the page's bitmap fill — `drawing-page-properties` with `draw:fill="bitmap"` +
  `draw:fill-image-name` + `style:repeat="stretch"`, and a named `<draw:fill-image>` in the
